items.title: Sainsbury's held blockbuster merger talks with rival Morrisons
items.summary: A merger between the two would be one of the biggest supermarket deals in more than five years and create a giant with a market share of 23.6 per cent.
items.body:
Sainsbury's held blockbuster merger talks with rival Morrisons
Sainsbury's held talks with smaller rival Morrisons over a potential merger before walking away earlier this year.
Sainsbury's reportedly held discussions with the private-equity-owned Morrisons between November 2025 and February of this year. The two supermarkets are no longer in active talks, the Financial Times reported.
A merger between the two would be one of the biggest supermarket deals in more than five years and create a giant with a market share of 23.6 per cent.
Britain’s number one supermarket Tesco holds 27.8 per cent of the grocery market, according to industry researchers Worldpanel.
A blockbuster deal would have come under fierce scrutiny from the competition watchdog, and Sainsbury's would have had to sell some of its shops to get the green light.
A merger between Sainsbury's and Morrisons would create a larger rival to market leader Tesco
Sainsbury’s attempt to buy Asda, the third-biggest grocer, in a £7.3billion takeover swoop was thwarted by the Competition and Markets Authority in 2019. They argued it would limit competition and discourage supermarkets from keeping prices low for customers.
Morrisons' owner, the private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice, remains open to a deal with a major rival, according to a Sky News report.
The grocer has been struggling to retain customers since its debt-fuelled £10billion takeover in 2021.
German discounters Aldi and Lidl have also posed a major threat to the traditional supermarket heavyweights, snapping up market share over the last fifteen years.
Aldi and Lidl's growing prominence - holding a combined total of just under 20 per cent of the market - could increase the likelihood of regulators giving Sainsbury's and Morrisons a green light, should they revive any discussions.
The reports come just a couple of months after Sainsbury’s agreed to sell its general merchandise business Argos to a new firm Swift Partners for £120million. It had originally bought it in a deal worth £1.4 billion in 2016.
Sainsbury's has been battling discounters through a focus on the food side of its business, appealing to customers with lower prices through its Nectar loyalty scheme and alternatives to dining out.
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons did not want to comment.

items.title: Jeremy Clarkson at Tory conference: ‘Why would anybody set up a business in this country?’
items.summary: Jeremy Clarkson hit out at the Labour government over its decision in 2024 to impose higher inheritance taxes on farming land two days before Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to call for a cut.  Clarkson said government officials failed to understand the impact of changes facing family farms as some owners had to sell [...]
items.body:
Jeremy Clarkson at Tory conference: ‘Why would anybody set up a business in this country?’
Jeremy Clarkson hit out at the Labour government over its decision in 2024 to impose higher inheritance taxes on farming land two days before Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to call for a cut.
Clarkson said government officials failed to understand the impact of changes facing family farms as some owners had to sell land.
Speaking on stage at the Conservative Party conference, the Diddly Squat farm owner said a decision to cap the 100 per cent agricultural property relief for inheritance tax at land and business assets totalling £1m. A government U-turn in late 2025 then led Labour ministers to raise the threshold to £2.5m.
“I think they didn’t understand it when they introduced it,” Clarkson said. “With a farm it’s completely different because you’d have to sell a bit of it, making it even less profitable, or you’d sell the whole lot.”
“It makes perfect sense for the way the countryside looks and our food supply system for farmers to pass it on to the only people who know how to do it, which is your kids.”
Reflecting on the challenges facing the farming sector, the former Top Gear start said: “Not every farmer has a quiz show to host on ITV, I think that’s the essence of it. If you’re an ordinary farmer, this is not just the weather, the attacks come from everywhere.”
Clarkson also revealed his “dream” of opening another pub outside the UK. “Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?” he asked on stage, adding: “I’ll see if I can do it abroad somewhere. I probably won’t, but I’m dreaming of it.”
His intervention comes ahead of the leader’s speech on Wednesday where Badenoch is expected to state her intention to cut inheritance taxes.
On the weekend, the Tory leader said inheritance taxes were “immoral”.
Badenoch’s possible tax announcement
The expected announcement, first reported in The Mail On Sunday and followed up elsewhere, could be a flagship announcement in Wednesday’s speech.
Inheritance tax of 40 per cent is levied on all estates with property worth more than £500,000. A couple can combine their allowances to pass on up to £1 million to their children.
The thresholds have been frozen for several years, dragging several more families into tax bands.
The Tories have so far announced spending cuts across welfare, aid and other areas worth more than £47bn. The party has allocated about half of the savings on tax cuts and the other half towards paying down the level of government debt.
Top shadow frontbenchers have insisted that the government would not make tax cuts until savings have been identified.
A party spokesman said rumours around an inheritance tax cut was “pure speculation”.
During his interview with the shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins, Clarkson also said regulations on farmers had cost businesses.
“I think if there were far fewer rules and regulations, yes there would be bad apples, there would be farmers I’m sure of it who would use DDT [a synthetic insecticide] or whatever, quietly do things which were reprehensible,” Clarkson said.
“But the vast majority, I don’t think they would. The farmers I know – they want to protect their farms because they want to hand them onto their children.”

items.title: Sainsbury’s and Morrisons held talks over blockbuster merger
items.summary: Sainsbury’s walked away from talks over a merger with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, shelving what would have been the biggest shake-up of the UK’s grocery market in decades.  The UK’s second-largest supermarket chain held preliminary talks with its private-equity-owned rival over a merger of the two firms between November 2025 and February this [...]
items.body:
Sainsbury’s and Morrisons held talks over blockbuster merger
Sainsbury’s walked away from talks over a merger with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year, shelving what would have been the biggest shake-up of the UK’s grocery market in decades.
The UK’s second-largest supermarket chain held preliminary talks with its private-equity-owned rival over a merger of the two firms between November 2025 and February this year, it is understood.
There are no active talks between the two sides but the two parties have not ruled out the possibility of discussions restarting in the future.
Sainsbury’s attempted to buy discount grocer Asda for £7.3bn in 2019, but had this deal blocked by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on the grounds it would reduce competition and push up prices for shoppers.
A deal to combine Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would inevitably draw the scrutiny of the CMA, which could force the firm to sell stores to soothe fears of lessened competition.
Sainsbury’s holds a 15.2 per cent share of the UK’s grocery market, while Morrisons has a 8.4 per cent share, according to Worldpanel by Numerator.
A combination of the two grocers would take their presence in the market to 23.6 per cent, widening the gap on Asda and Aldi but still below Tesco’s 27.8 per cent. Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons were first reported by Sky News’ Mark Kleinman.
Morrisons creaks under debt pile
Sainsbury’s chief executive Simon Roberts has pushed the supermarket chain to focus on its food sales, which jumped by three per cent to £8bn in the three months to June.
In July, the group sold Argos to Swift Partners for £120m, after buying the catalogue retailer for £1.4bn a decade ago.
Morrisons, the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket chain, has been weighed down by a huge debt pile since its takeover by the New-York based Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021.
The group’s net debt grew from £7.1bn to £7.5bn in the year to October 2025 but the grocer last month posted sales growth for the fifteenth consecutive quarter.
Rami Batiéh, who joined Morrisons in 2023, said his turnaround of the grocer is delivering a “broad-based improvement” across the group as he battles to cut costs and keep prices down.
Sainsbury’s operates more than 600 supermarkets and nearly 900 convenience stores. Morrisons runs about 500 supermarkets and more than 1,700 convenience outlets.
Shares in Sainsbury’s fell on news of the collapsed talks, to a loss of about 0.3 per cent at 322p.
Morrisons and Sainsbury’s declined to comment.

items.title: Greens pitch Zohran Mamdani-style $25.1bn plan to nationalise 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets
items.summary: Former MP and Greens Institute head, Max Chandler-Mather, says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery prices Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast More than 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather. Channelling New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan for publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the boss of the party’s thinktank, the Greens Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Continue reading...
items.body:
More than 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather.
Channelling New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan for publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the boss of the party’s thinktank, the Greens Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres.
The government would fund another 424 new supermarkets and 10 distribution centres, taking about 20% of the market share of commercial operators for the new non-profit network.
Chandler-Mather says the new stores – dubbed Fair Go Grocers – would save consumers as much as 22% on the average shop, or $60 per week for a four-person household. Heavy discounts would be put in place for essentials including fruit and vegetables, bread, milk and meat.
A statutory authority would be established to set prices each month, as well as minimum wholesale rates for suppliers. Its members would include experts in supermarket operations, nutrition and food science, and farming.
The federal government would pay for capital costs including land, construction, and acquisition, and stores would be located in areas of the highest need.
After an initial $25.1bn price tag over five years, Chandler-Mather says the stores would be self-funded and not require additional taxpayer cash.
By comparison, the federal government currently spends about $24bn each year on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.
“Kids are going to school hungry, families are skipping meals, people are cutting back on essentials, all because Labor has allowed Coles and Woolworths to jack up prices for extra profit, regardless of the human consequences,” Chandler-Mather said.
“Just like healthcare and education, food is essential to life. And just like Medicare and public schools, it’s time we had a public option for food.”
The proposal is similar to Mamdani’s plan for five city-owned and subsidised grocery stores, one in each of New York City’s boroughs, opening by 2029. Last month a local business group sued the Democratic Socialist mayor, arguing existing small grocery stores would be unable to compete.
The New Zealand Greens have a plan to nationalise 120 supermarkets and establish a new publicly owned chain called KiwiMark.
The Greens Institute commissioned pollsters YouGov to test public support for the proposal last month, with background on Mamdani’s plan for government-owned stores that cut out profits made by private corporations.
Voters were asked: Would you support or oppose publicly owned supermarkets being tried in Australia? A total of 84% said they strongly supported or somewhat supported the idea, while 16% somewhat or strongly opposed the idea.
Support was strongest among voters aged 25-34 (88%), among Greens voters (96%) and women (88%).
Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge, under pressure to spur enthusiasm and attention for the party, has welcomed the proposal, saying the Greens should be focused on improving the material conditions of individuals, the environment and community.
“A publicly owned supermarket with cheaper food is wildly popular, because it makes people’s lives better,” he told Guardian Australia.
“Of course this is the sort of policy that we should be discussing right now.”
Shoebridge said Mamdani’s message about the government needing to address the needs of citizens was working.
“When I talk to people, I hear about the dread they feel heading down the supermarket aisle, the shopping trolley feels like pushing a boulder up to the checkout,” he said.
“While 99% of us are paying more for food, and many are making decisions about enough food or some other essentials, the 1% who own Coles and Woolies are laughing.”
The competition watchdog has brought cases against both Coles and Woolworths over false or misleading representations about in-store discounts, and a report released last year found they were among the most profitable grocers in the world.
The Greens allege Labor’s new laws banning supermarkets from excessive pricing are ineffective and have not resulted in lower costs for consumers.

items.title: Frasers to convert Harvey Nichols Bristol and Leeds sites to Flannels
items.summary: Frasers cief executive Michael Murray, son-in-law of Mike Ashley, said he hopes to 'invest significant sums of money' in the famous Harvey Nichols store in Knightsbridge.
items.body:
Frasers to convert Harvey Nichols Bristol and Leeds sites to Flannels
The boss of Frasers has promised to bring Harvey Nichols’ London store ‘back to its former glory’ but will convert the Bristol and Leeds sites to Flannels stores.
Michael Murray, whose father-in-law billionaire Mike Ashley owns Frasers, said he hopes to ‘invest significant sums of money’ in the famous Harvey Nichols store in Knightsbridge.
Frasers launched its £40million rescue deal to buy the luxury department store chain after the chain warned it would run out of money if it failed to secure new investment.
The company, which also owns Sports Direct, has been focusing more on the luxury market in recent years, including taking stakes in fashion labels Burberry and Mulberry.
As part of the deal, Murray said Harvey Nichols' Bristol and Leeds stores will become Flannels, the luxury retailer owned by Frasers, with plans to refurbish the Edinburgh and Manchester shops. Harvey Nichols in Birmingham will shut.
Murray told Vogue Business: ‘For the London store, we are in talks with the Cadogan estate who own the freehold of Knightsbridge because we’re prepared to invest significant sums of money in that building as long as we can get the right terms with the landlord.
Frasers, which also owns Sports Direct, is putting more cash into its luxury brands - including buying the Harvey Nichols department store chain
'We want to do something truly remarkable in London and bring it back to its former glory.’
‘The [conversion] of the Bristol and Leeds Harvey Nichols stores to Flannels is part of the broader luxury strategy, allowing us to retain a presence in these locations while aligning them with the Flannels proposition,’ Murray said in an interview with Vogue Business.
In its 1990s heyday, fans of the London shop included Princess Diana and other fashion-forward 'Sloane Rangers'.
Mary Portas, the store's young creative director, made a deal with Absolutely Fabulous where its brash and boozy fashionista characters often mentioned the store and wore its clothes.
She transformed it into a trendy destination for the 'fashion-forward' with eye-catching window displays.
But it has failed to make a profit for five years after being hit by a downturn in tourism spending following the Covid pandemic and the removal of a VAT-free shopping scheme.
Earlier this year, PR guru Lynne Franks, who worked for Harvey Nicks in its heyday and inspired Jennifer Saunders’ character Eddy in Ab Fab, told This is Money the business should try to revive its ‘uniquely creative’ history.
She added: ‘The flagship has got to improve and become more unique with brands and marketing - it needs to get exciting. Make it fun, make people want to go there as a destination. Let’s see what happens.’
Murray said Harvey Nicks was an appealing acquisition ‘because it is very different from Flannels,’ and appealed to women predominately. ‘It works with a large array of brands beyond the major luxury brands, and has 200 years of heritage, which means it has value internationally,’ he said.
He pointed to existing Harvey Nichols shops in Riyadh, Dubai, Doha and Kuwait and said he was ‘looking at expansion opportunities through franchise partners,’ as well as ‘opportunities’ in Georgia and India to open ‘big’ shops with partners.
Murray also addressed anxiety over the acquisition following its brief takeover of online luxury marketplace Matchesfashion. Just three months after buying Matchesfashion in December 2023 for £52million, Frasers placed the company into administration with 273 job losses. This led to designer brands, including the likes of Burberry and Gucci, being owed a total of £36million.
He said: ‘The main difference is that Harvey Nichols is a physical retail business. Matches’s business model was very difficult. Free postage, free returns, low margin, huge overheads. 'When you cut it all back, there was not a lot there.’

items.title: Lidl's UK boss calls for planning reform as discounter eyes 50 new stores this year
items.summary: The British arm of the German discount giant has been opening new shops as it seeks to grow an even greater slice of the market. It has been using price cuts and loyalty offers to win share.
items.body:
Lidl's UK boss calls for planning reform as discounter eyes 50 new stores this year
The boss of Lidl UK has warned that planning delays are hitting investment and costing jobs as it outlines plans to open 50 new stores.
Chief executive Ryan McDonnell called for a shake-up ‘that creates a faster, more efficient planning process’ as he revealed the grocer’s UK sales hit £13billion.
The British arm of the German discount giant, which recently overtook Morrisons to become the country's fifth-largest grocer, is seeking to grow its market share further with a £600million investment into new shops.
The company has also been trying to win more customers by price cuts and promotions, including through its Lidl Plus loyalty app.
It said revenue rose 10.8 per cent to £13billion over the year to February 28, 2026 – thanks to 40 new shops which opened during the period. Operating profits rose 9.9 per cent to £345million.
It said it won 43 million new shoppers and continued to be the UK’s ‘fastest-growing bricks-and-mortar supermarket.’
Lidl sold 486 million more products, with growth across fresh meat and fruit and vegetables, and said it invested a total of £315million into affordable prices.
Grocery price wars: German discounter Lidl has been poaching customers from other supermarkets
It comes as traditional supermarkets have been on the defensive and launched their own slew of price cuts over the past two years.
Sales have benefited from a shift that has seen Brits opt to ‘dine in’ rather than eating out at pubs and restaurants amid high living costs.
Lidl’s ‘premium deluxe’ range rose 12 per cent as McDonnell said ‘customers are increasingly looking to trade up and treat themselves at home.’
Boss McDonnell said there were ‘hundreds more opportunities for stores’ as the group looks to expand its footprint in key cities such as London and Glasgow.
But he added: ‘Any planning delays or administrative bottlenecks can of course slow down crucial investments, job creation, and local economic growth.
‘We would welcome reform that creates a faster, more efficient planning process.’
His remarks echo those of Next boss Lord Wolfson, who argued that the planning system is a larger hurdle for economic growth than business rates.
It is not the first time Lidl has railed against delays at local authorities leading to protracted planning processes.
Earlier this year, Richard Taylor, Lidl’s UK chief real estate officer, said the UK was ‘stuck in the slow lane’ and a ‘lack of consistency’ across planning authorities had delayed store openings.
McDonnell’s comments come a couple of months after the competition watchdog said that Aldi and Lidl should not be able to block rival supermarkets from opening close to their shops. They are set to be included with other large supermarkets - after an explosion in growth over the last decade.
McDonnell said the group ‘embrace that fair market competition’ and said he was not concerned that the changes would ‘slow our momentum as we continue expanding the store network.’
The business is ‘gearing up’ for ‘our biggest Christmas yet,’ he said.
McDonnell added: ‘Our performance is a clear testament to the trust that millions of customers place in us every week as a direct result of the dedication of our colleagues right across the country.
‘As we grow, our focus doesn't shift - we're constantly investing in low prices, high quality, and maximum value for our customers.’
Only Ocado, which sells groceries online, has been achieving better growth in recent months, according to industry researchers at Worldpanel.
Lidl overtook Morrisons as the country’s fifth biggest grocer in May.
Market researchers at Worldpanel said that Lidl held 8.7 per cent of the market over the three months to September 6, from 8.3 per cent a year ago
Its sales rose 8 per cent to £3.16billion over the period – eclipsing sales growth at rival Aldi, where sales grew just 0.7 per cent in the same period.
Lidl has had an impressive ascent, as 20 years ago it made up just 1.4 per cent of the market.

items.body:
The Very Group, which operates digital retailers Very and Littlewoods, has partnered with Made With Intent to enhance the digital shopping journey.
The new partnership will see Very offer its customers a more personalised experience than ever before. By using over 800 behavioural signals, Made With Intent’s agentic decision engine predicts customer’s intent in real-time, helping to decide what they see and when.
All based on customer behaviour and intention, Very will now be able to spotlight discount offers unique to customers based on individual shopping trends, as well as provide prompts at crucial moments throughout the shopping experience.
Made With Intent’s engine is built on a proprietary model and optimisation AI agent that work together to allocate experiences across hundreds of intent combinations, learning what works for which visitors and contexts then applying it to future sessions.
Sarah Hanna, digital director at The Very Group, commented: “Made With Intent’s agentic platform unlocks fast paced, scalable real-time personalisation that can be executed to help enhance the customer experience, ultimately influencing our commercial KPIs. In fact, in the first month of the partnership, we’ve already seen promising results including revenue per customer increasing by a fifth in one of our agentic strategies, and an uplift in overall conversion.
“Made With Intent gives our ecommerce team a brand-new lever that they can effortlessly activate to make a difference on what our customers see and when – whether that’s one-off discounts or personalised payment options. It’s all about giving customers the right experience at the right time.”
David Mannheim, founder of Made With Intent, added: “Personalisation is a word you hear a lot when talking about retail, especially online. Our agentic AI decision engine gives innovative teams like Very’s the scale that’s needed to deliver more impactful, hyper-personalised customer experiences. Our goal has always been to move ecommerce away from generic, static experiences designed for everyone towards something more personalised and real-time. Not only because it is a better experience for visitors, but because it finds new growth, and we’re excited to be on this journey with The Very Group.”

items.body:
For 2026, Hotel Chocolat launches new products to support the growing opportunity the occasion brings to premium brands, with options designed for hosting, sharing, and gifting.
The Halloween 2026 collection includes new Skull Lick, Oozy Eye Selectors, and Fright Night Selectors, alongside returning favourites: Grim Treater Skulls, Halloween Nice Slice, and Boo Boxes. All available now in-store and online.
The occasion is also being marked in the Velvetiser Café, with the Cherry Scary Sundae (topped with a Grim Treater Skull) available from 2nd October.
The Grim Treaters – £12.95
In each box, you’ll find four chocolate skulls with two of each playful designs and flavours:
Skull 1 – Milk chocolate with hazelnut praline, caramel éclat and feuilletine.
Skull 2 – High cacao caramel chocolate with pecan praline, dark chocolate with hazelnut praline, caramel éclat and feuilletine.
Boo Boxes – £9.95
Fiendish boxes filled with 16 individually wrapped chocolate characters. Perfect for trick-or-treaters or gifting to little ones (and the young at heart). Choose from milk chocolates within Carvin the Pumpkin, solid caramel-milk in Cryptopher the Vampire, or dark chocolates guarded by Wingston the Bat.
Frightful Bites Halloween Box – £17.95
Filled with a mix of 14 classic and spinetingling seasonal recipes, including caramels, pralines and solid chocolates. Do you dare try our gloriously gory Oozy Eyes? They’re served in 36% white or 40% milk chocolate, both loaded with molten red caramel.
Yumpkin – £6.95
If you don’t fancy pumpkin carving this year (or just want something a little tastier), pick our Halloween Yumpkin instead: cast in smooth and mellow 40% milk chocolate. Ribbon-tied and ready to display (or devour)
Grim Treater Chocolate Lick – £2.95
Our grinning Grim Treater cast in wickedly smooth 40% milk chocolate.
Fright Night Chocolate Selector – £4.65
Scarily smooth white peanut pralines and 50% milk chocolate ganache’s.
Cherry Scary Sundae – £7.50 (£6.00 for VIP.ME)
Ice Cream of the Gods with a zing of sour cherry all topped with cherry sauce, milk crisp pearls and a Halloween themed chocolate.
Two new drinking chocolates have also been introduced today: Walnut and Roasted Almond, priced at £14.95 each, join the core drinking chocolate range within the Exquisitely Nutty Love Match.
- Walnut: Bold and beautifully balanced. We chose walnut for its earthy depth and complex character. Think rich, near-savoury nuttiness that lingers on the palate, elevated by the equally deep, nuanced notes of our signature 70% dark chocolate. A statement of sophistication for your autumn drinking chocolate capsule collection (and it’s vegan too!)
- Roasted Almond:Take a sip and succumb to the creamy allure of real, roasted almond. We drape it in equal layers of mellow 36% white and 40% milk chocolate, each chosen for their ability to complement its delicate, nutty profile. Warming, comforting, like slipping into a soft, chunky knit on a crisp autumn day.

items.title: Unitas Local Living adds new £1 PMP confectionery line to portfolio
items.summary: Unitas is launching a new six-strong confectionery line to its Local Living portfolio, giving shoppers a choice of classic sugar confectionery favourites at independent retailers. Launching on 5 October, the range includes Fizzy Mix, Giant Fizzy Strawbs, Mini Pencils, Tangy Mix, Sour Snakes and Party Mix,… This story continues at Unitas Local Living adds new £1 PMP confectionery line to portfolio Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Launching on 5 October, the range includes Fizzy Mix, Giant Fizzy Strawbs, Mini Pencils, Tangy Mix, Sour Snakes and Party Mix, with each variety available in a £1 price marked 130g sharing bag.
The new Local Living range addition comprises six varieties of sharing sweets. Each SKU delivers more than 30% POR, while the £1 price marked format clearly communicates the accessible price point.
Supporting the launch is Unitas’ “Our £1 just got sweeter” campaign, designed to bring the new range to life in-store and firmly place its accessible price point front of mind for shoppers.
The confectionery launch is the latest addition to the growing Local Living own brand range, following the recent introduction of a new home baking line, with plans to further expand the category with the addition of self-raising flour and plain flour, which will be coming soon.
The continued expansion of Local Living reflects Unitas’ focus on developing its own brand offer across key everyday categories.
Milan Pinnock, own brand marketing manager at Unitas, said: “Confectionery is a key impulse category for independent retailers, so we wanted to create a range that makes it easy for retailers to offer shoppers plenty of choice at an affordable price.

items.title: High street needs investment to save UK economy almost £16bn by 2040
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Only one in 10 (10%) Britons put hearing in their top three health priorities, and just 7% say that they invest most of their time and money in it compared to other areas of their health, according to new research from Specsavers. The research reveals that more than a third (35%) consider eye health to […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Only one in 10 (10%) Britons put hearing in their top three health priorities, and just 7% say that they invest most of their time and money in it compared to other areas of their health, according to new research from Specsavers.
The research reveals that more than a third (35%) consider eye health to be important, but only 28% invest their time and money in it – pointing to a gap between importance and investment that persists across every generation.
Britons rank sleep, diet, exercise and mental health above their sight and hearing, despite the fact that losing either sense can have lifelong consequences. And the scale of the problem is growing – new analysis from Development Economics commissioned by Specsavers has found that sight loss cases will rise from 2.38m to 3.11m by 2040. As well as this, 19.2 million adults have hearing loss in the UK today, and cases of significant hearing loss are expected to rise by 16% by 2040.
Part of the issue is that Britons are hesitant to get tested – half (50%) wouldn’t book a test unless something felt wrong, and nearly half (47%) of those assume that their sight and hearing are fine until symptoms show. This is despite many recognising the importance of sight and hearing care to their overall wellbeing.
While they may not feel that they need to get tested right away, the amount of people living with sight and hearing loss by 2040 is projected to rise by millions. And according to the British Academy of Audiology, of the 6.7m UK adults experiencing hearing loss that could benefit from a hearing aid, only around 2 million currently use one. Hearing and sight issues already costs the UK £106 billion – this is projected to rise to £126 billion by 2040 if changes aren’t made to the accessibility of care within communities.
The research has uncovered that time and proximity are key barriers stopping people getting their hearing and sight tested. People don’t travel more than 30 minutes for a sight or hearing test, with over a quarter (28%) reporting that lack of time is contributing to their delaying or avoiding an eye test, and 22% feeling the same way when it comes to a hearing test.
The high street still plays a vital role in people’s lives and to their healthcare. 90% say that opticians are essential to their high street, making it the same importance as the post office or bank, and daily high street visitors are three times more likely to get their sight and hearing tested than people who rarely go (73% of regular high street visitors get tested compared to 26% of non-regulars).
Carina Hummel, managing director Optics UK&ROI at Specsavers, said: “Regardless of where people live or their circumstances, it’s so important that we create and preserve easy access to quality sight and hearing care. We need to encourage people to treat their eye and ear health the same way they would treat other areas of their health – a routine check-up, not just booking an appointment when something feels “off”.
“Offering easy access to care via high street appointments and home visits improves health outcomes and wellbeing, ensuring that we are looking after ourselves. For adults, that looks like having a sight test every two years, and a hearing test every 18 months to two years for people over 40. Appointments don’t take long and can ultimately help to detect and treat any conditions sooner.”

Premium craftsmanship is the cornerstone of the […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Launching on 8th October, the premium collection brings together clothsurgeon’s unique blend of luxury streetwear and Savile Row expertise with John Lewis’s trusted heritage to create pieces that are thoughtfully constructed and refined.
Designed as a complete capsule wardrobe, the collection spans tailoring, outerwear, knitwear, jersey, and accessories. Premium craftsmanship is the cornerstone of the collection, featuring Italian wool tailoring, luxury leather outerwear and accessories, brushed cashmere knits, Japanese selvedge denim and Portuguese jersey.
Several of clothsurgeon’s bestsellers have been reinterpreted for the collection, including the brand’s signature double breasted blazer and tuxedo. Trademark clothsurgeon details, such as custom buttons, tapes and linings, feature throughout the collection, seamlessly blend with John Lewis’ expertise in tailoring to produce a collection of elevated essentials.
On the collection, clothsurgeon Founder and Creative Director Rav Matharu MBE says: “It’s wonderful to have the opportunity to work with such a highly respected British institution as John Lewis. Our aim was to create a collection focused on contemporary tailored menswear for all occasions and settings, offering a timeless wardrobe for the modern man.”
Sartorial elements are woven into every style, even the most streetwear inspired pieces, as the collection bridges both influences. From the checked bomber jacket featuring a clothsurgeon signature kidney collar guard and welt pockets, to the brushed cashmere crew knits detailed with a distinct trio of buttons, the collection is centred around an impeccable attention to detail.
Hero pieces include an Italian wool-blend tuxedo, a leather utility jacket and a cobalt blue brushed cashmere crew knit, which injects a pulse of energy through the collection. The line up is completed with accessories, including ties, a pony hair belt and in the same striking cobalt, a printed silk scarf and a baseball cap.
The collection extends into footwear with a range exclusively designed for clothsurgeon by British shoemaker Grenson, featuring a soft grain leather trainer, a Cuban heel ankle boot, and a pony hair on loafer.

items.body:
Launching today (5 October), BrewDog gives the nation reasons to ‘Choose Craft’ in a high-profile campaign celebrating craft beer, brewers and beer lovers, and championing quality ingredients, brewing passion and community spirit.
The highlight of Choose Craft is impactful murals in prominent locations in Manchester and Edinburgh, supported by static and digital adverts distributed across major nationwide railway and underground stations, roadside locations and proximity advertising close to major stockists.
With examples including keeping the empty cans just because you like the artwork, waiting to ensure your favourite beer is at the perfect temperature before drinking it and knowing the flavour profile so intimately that you can tell the difference in varying batches – all reasons to choose craft.
John Beasley, chief marketing officer, comments: “Choose Craft is our commitment to the future of the category. It not only celebrates everything that makes craft beer worth choosing: the passion, care and creativity of brewers, but also the community who make the category so special.
“The creative is an observation of this community’s shared obsession for great tasting beers, quality ingredients and brewing excellence that is like no other.
“Following our ‘Under New Ownership’ campaign, which signalled BrewDog’s renewed focus on what it does best, Choose Craft moves onto the future with optimism, reminding our fans what we all love about craft beer and looking ahead with confidence.
“This is a hugely dynamic category, and we take our position as the leading craft beer brand seriously. The new campaign is a promise from BrewDog to keep brewing and serving some of the best beers in the world so that beer lovers continue to choose craft.”

Menswear retailer Suit Direct is set to open a new store at Festival Place in Basingstoke on Friday 2nd October, bringing its range of tailoring, suits and casualwear to shoppers in Basingstoke and the surrounding area.
Located at Unit 15 Wesley Walk, Festival Place Shopping Centre, Basingstoke, RG21 7BE, the new store will offer customers a dedicated space to shop Suit Direct’s collection of suits, tailoring, casualwear and accessories, with expert in-store advice and personalised styling available.
A new destination for menswear in Basingstoke
The new Festival Place store has been designed to offer a more personal approach to menswear shopping, with customers able to receive expert guidance on fit, fabric and styling from the Suit Direct team. From special events to everyday wear, customers will find a wide selection of tailoring, occasionwear and casualwear all under one roof.
Lisa Tobin, Head of Retail Elevation at Suit Direct, said:
“We are delighted to be opening our new Suit Direct store at Festival Place; it’s a fantastic location for us to bring Suit Direct to the local community and make finding the right outfit for every occasion easier than ever.
“Whether it’s a wedding, a special celebration, an important work moment, or simply updating your everyday wardrobe, we want our customers to feel confident that they can find something that works for them. Our new store brings together a wide choice of suits, tailoring and casualwear, giving customers the flexibility to dress for every part of their week.
“What really sets the Suit Direct experience apart is the personal service we offer in store. Our team has a genuine passion for tailoring and understands how important the right fit can be. From finding the right cut and fabric through to those final finishing touches, we’re here to offer expert advice and make the experience feel personal and enjoyable.
“We’re really looking forward to welcoming the Basingstoke community into our new store. We want it to be a place where customers can discover great style, get expert advice and leave feeling confident in a new outfit that’s just right for them.”
Suit Direct’s UK expansion
The Basingstoke opening forms part of Suit Direct’s wider expansion across the UK, with the retailer continuing to develop its presence in prominent city-centre and shopping-centre locations.
The new Festival Place store will feature Suit Direct’s latest retail design and merchandising, alongside the brand’s selection of tailoring, casualwear, accessories and premium menswear brands, including Ted Baker and Antique Rogue.
Customers will be able to shop suits and formalwear alongside more relaxed pieces including knitwear, chinos and other everyday wardrobe staples, creating a destination for menswear across occasions and seasons.
The new Suit Direct store at Festival Place will open on Friday 2nd October.

items.title: Lidl GB’s sales soar by over 10%, helped by price cuts and Deluxe range
items.summary: German-owned supermarket beats Morrisons to become fifth largest grocer in Great Britain Business live – latest updates Lidl’s sales in Great Britain jumped 10% to more than £13bn this year, as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables and snapped up its Deluxe range. Pre-tax profit at the German-owned supermarket’s arm in Great Britain grew by 30% to £245.5m in the year ended in February, up from £156.8m in the previous year. Continue reading...
items.body:
Lidl’s sales in Great Britain jumped 10% to more than £13bn this year, as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables and snapped up its Deluxe range.
Pre-tax profit at the German-owned supermarket’s arm in Great Britain grew by 30% to £245.5m in the year ended in February, up from £156.8m in the previous year.
Shoppers have flocked to discounters such as Lidl amid rising food inflation, with in-store prices stepping up to an annual rate of 1.5% in August, up from 0.9% in July. Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%.
Lidl said it had spent £315m on price cuts and promotions such as its “pick of the week” product, while increasing numbers of shoppers were choosing its Deluxe upmarket food range.
“Deluxe sales are up 12% as more households dine in rather than eat out,” the Lidl GB chief executive, Ryan McDonnell, said. “Customers are looking to trade up and treat themselves at home.”
This year Lidl beat Morrisons to become the fifth largest grocer in Great Britain, with its market share hitting 8.6% in the 12 weeks to 17 May, according to figures from the market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.
That compared with an 8.3% share for Morrisons, which increased its sales by just 1.3% compared with a year earlier.
Aldi and Lidl have grown rapidly, thanks partly to slowing performance at Asda and Morrisons after both were acquired in debt-fuelled private equity deals.
However, Aldi’s growth has slowed recently as Tesco and Sainsbury’s have offered more savings via their loyalty schemes and ranges that match the German discounter on price.
Lidl said performance at its loyalty programme Lidl Plus had been particularly strong, with a 23% rise in participants this year.
The analyst Clive Black, the vice-chair at the broker Shore Capital, said that was in contrast to Aldi “where management has a clear strategy to deride such programmes”.
Aldi is the only big supermarket chain in the UK that does not operate a loyalty scheme.
This month the boss of Aldi UK, Giles Hurley, criticised some loyalty discounts that he said tricked customers by starting with “unrealistically high prices” that then dropped.
He told BBC News that discounts were helpful “when they’re real and when they show realistic reductions”, but criticised what he described as unrealistic reductions which “dupe customers”.
The UK’s competition watchdog investigated loyalty pricing schemes at supermarkets in 2024 and found that shoppers “almost always make a genuine saving”.

With families increasingly investing in personalised keepsakes and traditions that can be enjoyed year after year, Mamas & Papas has revealed its top 10 Christmas must-haves for 2026 – from a personalised advent calendar and Christmas sacks to baby’s first decorations and festive knitwear.
The leading nursery retailer has more than doubled the number of personalised clothing styles in this year’s collection and expanded the service across soft toys for the first time.
It comes as its bestselling advent calendar sold out before November last year and more than 90% of customers chose to personalise their Christmas sacks.
It reflects a growing appetite for products that become part of annual festive family rituals – whether that’s hanging the same decoration on the tree each year, sharing a Christmas Eve box together, or counting down to 25th December with a personalised advent calendar.
Mamas & Papas is also launching new gift boxes for the first time next month to make Christmas gifting even easier and more memorable for friends and family. Available in-store and online, shoppers can handpick their favourite gifts and have them wrapped in a hand-illustrated gift box, ready to place under the tree or send directly to loved ones’ doors. A gift-packing service will also be available to online and in-store shoppers throughout the festive season, adding an extra touch of magic to special gifts.
The full Christmas range launches in-store and online on Monday 5th October.
Sonia Kelly, Senior Product Director at Mamas & Papas, said: “We know Christmas is about so much more than gifts – it’s about the moments families share and the traditions children carry with them into adulthood. We’ve seen a real appetite for personalised keepsakes that become part of those annual rituals.
“That’s why we’ve made personalisation a much bigger focus across this year’s collection, giving families even more opportunities to create meaningful traditions and treasured keepsakes they’ll use year after year. After our personalised advent calendar sold out before November last year, we’re encouraging parents who have their eye on a particular item to shop early to avoid missing out.”

items.body:
Global Parent-care brand, Tommee Tippee, has joined forces with Disney, featuring designs of the much-loved bear, Winnie the Pooh (and friends), and for the very first time, this special collaboration brings a fresh, contemporary approach to the Hundred Acre Wood, combining playful design, bold colour and iconic Pooh moments.
To celebrate the centenary of everyone’s favourite Pooh bear, the joyful new range for babies and toddlers features the beloved illustrations of Disney Winnie the Pooh and friends, giving Tommee Tippee’s trusted feeding essentials a playful new look through cheerful prints, warm patterns and a vivid colour palette.
Created to cater for everything from little ones’ adventure-filled sips to soothing moments as sweet as honey, the range adds a touch of imagination and much-loved nostalgia to families’ everyday routines. It has been designed to make the most of those everyday moments, much like Winnie the Pooh himself does.
The collection includes Natural Start® bottles accepted by 95% of babies,** soothers that help 96% of parents feel reassured their baby is calm and settled,** and toddler-proof cups made for every sip and adventure.
The new collection includes:
Decorated Natural Start® Bottles x2 (260ml & 150ml) (0m+)
Bringing even more joy to feeding time with Natural Start® bottles featuring charming Disney Winnie the Pooh illustrations, playful patterns and vibrant colours.
Combining beautiful design with trusted feeding innovation, the bottles are designed to make switching between breast and bottle easier, with a breast-like teat that supports a natural latch and a built-in anti-colic valve to help keep babies comfortable at every feed.
Ultimate Fit Soothers (0-6m, 6-18m, 18-36m)
The Disney Winnie the Pooh inspired soothers featuring Disney Winnie the Pooh designs are thoughtfully designed to keep little ones comfortable at every stage.
Featuring joyful colours and beloved Disney Winnie the Pooh artwork, the orthodontic soothers have a vented symmetrical silicone teat which compresses to be gentle on developing teeth and gums, and an any way up shield with air holes to help improve airflow and reduce moisture build- up.
Active Spout Cup (12m+)
Helping little explorers stay hydrated on every adventure, the beautifully designed insulated straw cups feature playful artwork and patterns.
Combining practical innovation with imaginative design, the leak-proof cups are engineered to prevent spills and drops, with easy-grab handles for little hands and double-wall insulation to help keep drinks cooler for longer while toddlers play, learn and explore.
Starter Cup (4m+)
Supporting little ones on their drinking journey, the training cup features bright, bold colours and character-led Disney Winnie the Pooh artwork.
Designed to help babies build confidence as they learn to sip, the cup combines a leak- and shake-proof design with easy-grip handles, a gentle yet durable spout, and a removable lid to keep the spout clean, bringing a little extra joy to every learning moment.
Active Straw Cup (12m+)
Making hydration more fun, the insulated flip-straw cup features playful Disney Winnie the Pooh artwork and patterns, inspired by adventure and imagination.
Designed for little hands and busy toddlers, the leak-proof cup combines practical features including a durable bite-resistant straw, flip-down hygienic cover and double-wall insulation to help keep drinks cool, bringing a little extra joy to every sip.
Rachel Costello, Group Marketing Director at Tommee Tippee, said: “We’re delighted to collaborate with Disney Baby to celebrate 100 years of Disney Winnie the Pooh with a collection that brings together two much-loved brands with a shared connection to generations of families. At Tommee Tippee, we’re committed to creating trusted, thoughtfully designed products that make everyday moments with little ones that little bit easier and more joyful. This special collection pairs our much-loved feeding and soothing essentials with the timeless charm, warmth and spirit of adventure that Winnie the Pooh has inspired for generations. We hope the collection brings a touch of wonder to those precious everyday moments, from feeding and soothing to supporting little ones as they learn, grow and explore.”
Tommee Tippee’s new collaboration with Disney Baby builds on the success of its BINIBAMBA and Morris & Co. collaboration earlier this year, continuing the brand’s commitment to pairing exceptional design with everyday baby essentials that parents know and trust.
The collection spans baby and toddler with its fun patterns making everyday moments even sweeter. The range will be available on Tommee Tippee and Boots online from October 1st.

items.body:
Waitrose has announced an exclusive new partnership with renowned chef and seafood champion Rick Stein, his first ever supermarket food range. Designed to bring the flavours of iconic coastal dining into the comfort of your home, the collection features nine restaurant-quality, British sourced fish and seafood dishes, and will land on Waitrose shelves and online from 7 October.
Every dish in the range celebrates responsibly sourced British fish, combining premium ingredients with Rick Stein’s decades of culinary expertise and passion for simple, brilliant seafood. From effortless mid-week suppers to indulgent weekend feasts, the range has been designed to meet customers’ demand for exceptional seafood, which is straightforward and stress-free to cook.
Rick Stein comments: “In the new range with Waitrose, we’ve focused on fish you can feel confident about – thoughtfully sourced, full of flavour, and something to be enjoyed at home without any fuss. There’s a real sense of the British coast running through it, particularly Cornwall where it all began for me, but also the influence of the many places I’ve travelled and the flavours I’ve come to love along the way. For me, it’s always been about keeping things simple – great fish, good ingredients, and letting them speak for themselves.”
The new Rick Stein with Waitrose range brings true culinary innovation to Waitrose shelves with a series of market firsts. Showcasing pioneering en papillote packaging, the Hake and Scottish Loch Trout steam-cook effortlessly for peak delicacy and flavour. Meanwhile, the range’s Panko White Fish Gratin offers a fresh take on a traditional fish pie, using Panko breadcrumbs instead of mash and containing rich Scottish smoked haddock, which has been smoked in one of the last of its kind, heritage brick chimneys in Grimsby, via a century-old technique.
The new range features year-round coastal classics alongside special festive showstoppers which will be landing on shelves in time for Christmas.
- British Hake En Papillote – with a roasted red pepper dressing & tarragon mayo, £14
- Scottish Loch Trout En Papillote -with British samphire & brown butter with capers & lemon, £14
- Panko White Fish Gratin – in a savoury, creamy lemon and miso béchamel sauce, £14
- Monkfish & Whiting Indonesian Curry – a vibrant, aromatic classic packed with flavour, £16
- Shetland Mussels with XO Sauce – rich, savoury, and perfectly spiced, £6.50
- Cornish Sardines – with a vibrant, zesty marinade of lemon, parsley & chilli – keep an eye out for this seasonal special, available from launch until January £6.50
Festive additions – Landing in time for Christmas
- British Lobster & Crab Thermidor Shells – a decadent, indulgent starter, £12
- Scottish Traditionally Smoked Salmon- Thickly sliced, dry cured with Cornish sea salt
- £7.50
- Scottish Salmon, British Lobster & Crab Thermidor En Croute- the ultimate festive centrepiece, available via Waitrose Entertaining, £53
Paul Gamble, senior development chef at Waitrose, comments: “Collaborating with Rick to bring this range to life has been an incredible experience. Rick’s passion for seafood is legendary, and our goal was to capture that signature restaurant magic while making it completely effortless for our food loving customers to cook at home. We’ve focused on showcasing the absolute best of responsibly sourced British fish. We’ve paired delicate flavours like Scottish Loch Trout with rich brown butter and British samphire, and given classic white fish an unexpected twist with miso and lemon béchamel. Whether you’re an avid home cook or intimidated by preparing fish, these dishes deliver incredible, restaurant-quality results every single time.”
Waitrose and Rick Stein share a longstanding commitment to championing British fisheries and responsible sourcing. All nine products feature fish caught or farmed to strict welfare and environmental standards, ensuring customers can enjoy exceptional quality, as well high-quality protein, vitamin D, and omega-3 while supporting responsibly sourced British seafood.
The Waitrose x Rick Stein range will be available in 210 Waitrose branches and online at Waitrose.com from 7 October. The festive additions of the range will start to launch from 25 November for Smoked Salmon, and the Thermidor shells and Salmon, Lobster and Crab Wellington will be available from 18th December.

items.body:
Frasers Group today announces the beginning of a new era with Frasers Group Luxury – a luxury ecosystem spanning the UK and U.S with ambitions to grow globally.
Frasers Group Luxury combines a portfolio of distinctive luxury businesses, digital capabilities, and investments with long-standing strategic brand partners at its core. Built on more than a decade of experience in the sector, and underpinned by the trust from strategic brand partners, Frasers Group Luxury represents the next phase of the Group’s luxury strategy. It combines the expertise and reach of Frasers Group with the commercial discipline that underpins the wider business.
More than a collection of retailers, Frasers Group Luxury brings together iconic UK brands FLANNELS and Harvey Nichols, alongside The Webster in the U.S., spanning two major luxury markets and creating a platform for future global growth.
● FLANNELS was acquired by Frasers Group in 2017 and has since established itself as a leading destination for ‘New Luxury’ in the UK, with more than 80 stores across the country.
● With the addition of The Webster in 2025, Frasers Group entered the U.S. luxury market. One year into the partnership, The Webster has strengthened the Group’s international presence, bringing together an exceptional portfolio of the world’s most sought-after luxury brands. It has also seen continued investment into The Webster’s store estate in Bal Harbour, South Beach and New York.
● Harvey Nichols joined Frasers Group in 2026, adding one of the UK’s most recognised luxury retailers, with almost 200 years of heritage and longstanding relationships with leading global brands.
This portfolio spans different expressions of luxury retail, alongside strategic investments in the wider luxury landscape, including Mulberry, Burberry, HUGO BOSS and HULCAN’s Mile. Frasers Group Luxury is designed to support brand partners at every stage of their growth – unlocking opportunities, reaching new audiences, entering new markets and creating lasting long-term value.
Michael Murray, Frasers Group chief executive officer, commented: “Luxury has been a core pillar of Frasers Group for more than a decade, starting with FLANNELS and growing into a
profitable £1b+ luxury ecosystem in just 10 years. With over 100 stores across the UK and U.S., we’ve built the expertise, scale, and brand relationships to support our next phase of growth.
Our ambition is clear: to continue scaling Frasers Group Luxury globally through organic expansion, acquisitions, and strategic investments, creating long-term value for our brand partners, customers, and the Group.”
Julia Goddard, Harvey Nichols chief executive officer, said: “Frasers Group provides Harvey Nichols with the expertise, support, and pace to build on our heritage and shape our next chapter. Its understanding of luxury, combined with a strong operational and commercial approach, gives us the confidence to invest, evolve and build for the long term.”
Laure Heriard Dubreuil, The Webster founder, added: “As we mark one year since The Webster joined Frasers Group, I feel tremendous excitement about what lies ahead. We have already accomplished so much together, and the Group’s support is helping bring the vision I have long held for The Webster to life on a greater scale.
That momentum is taking shape in Bal Harbour, where this November we will unveil our newly renovated store as part of the Bal Harbour Shops West expansion, after calling our original location home since 2013. As we look toward our 20th anniversary, our sights are also set on renovating our iconic South Beach flagship and bringing new life to 1220 Collins Avenue, where it all began. Michael and I share a belief in the enduring value of physical retail, and that alignment gave us confidence in the partnership from the start.
I want The Webster to remain a place where time stops – where clients can discover something unexpected, receive the highest level of personal service, and enjoy exclusive products and experiences created with our brand partners. That vision extends to our growing the footprint of our partnership with renowned hair salon David Mallett, which operates within our SoHo, New York store. At the same time, the recent relaunch of our website is creating new ways to connect with clients wherever they are. Together with Frasers Group, we are building on The Webster’s strong foundation and shaping its future, in our stores and online.”
Paris Fashion Week will provide the backdrop for the first Frasers Group Luxury evening, bringing together its luxury community of key brand partners, designers, talent, industry figures and international press. The gathering reflects the breadth of the business today, from luxury retail to investment and brand partnerships and marks the beginning of its next phase of growth across the UK and U.S.

items.title: Your shoppers are loyal, just not necessarily to you. Here’s how to win more of their spend

As shoppers increasingly spread their spend across supermarkets, Simon Betts, UK country leader at Catalina, looks at what retailers can do to win a greater share of the basket this Golden Quarter, and why more promotions aren’t necessarily the answer I’ve spent more than 20 years working in retail, including on the retailer side at […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
As shoppers increasingly spread their spend across supermarkets, Simon Betts, UK country leader at Catalina, looks at what retailers can do to win a greater share of the basket this Golden Quarter, and why more promotions aren’t necessarily the answer
I’ve spent more than 20 years working in retail, including on the retailer side at Tesco, and there’s one word we’ve probably talked about more than almost any other and that’s loyalty.
How do we get customers to come back? How do we increase frequency? How do we win a bigger share of their weekly shop?
As we head into the Golden Quarter, those questions become even more important, but we need to be realistic about what loyalty looks like in 2026. Shoppers haven’t stopped being loyal, they’ve just become much more willing to spread that loyalty around.
New YouGov research we commissioned at Catalina found 28% of UK adults are shopping across multiple supermarkets more often than they were a year ago. The same proportion are spending more time searching for promotions and discounts, while one in three (34%) are using loyalty card discounts more often.
For retailers, that should ring a few alarm bells. The customer standing in your store on Tuesday might be in your competitor’s on Friday. Having your loyalty card in their wallet or your app on their phone doesn’t necessarily mean you have their loyalty or their whole basket.
The opportunity for retailers is to use the data they already have to understand those changing behaviours and give shoppers a genuinely relevant reason to choose them again. And, as our research shows, that doesn’t necessarily mean throwing more promotions at them.
Seven in ten adults (70%) told us they would be more likely to shop at their supermarket of choice if it offered personalised rewards based on products they regularly buy, whether that’s money-off coupons, bonus loyalty points or free products.
When we asked shoppers to choose the single most effective way a supermarket could keep them loyal, money-off coupons for products they regularly buy came out on top, selected by 29%.
The important words there are products they regularly buy. That’s the difference between simply discounting and delivering something genuinely valuable.
Give me 50p off something I have never bought and don’t want, and I’m probably going to ignore it. Give me money off something that goes into my basket every week and suddenly you’ve given me a reason to come back.
It sounds incredibly simple, but relevance is where the real opportunity lies.
Every transaction tells you something about a shopper – what they buy, how frequently they visit, what they buy together, when their habits start to change and what brings them back.
At Catalina, this is what we spend our time looking at – billions of transactions that help us understand what people actually do, rather than relying purely on what they tell us they do.
And increasingly, what we’re seeing is that there isn’t really a ‘typical shopper’. Someone can buy broadly the same basket for years and then suddenly change. Cost pressures, a new health goal or a change in family circumstances can all shift behaviour. We’re even seeing major trends such as GLP-1 weight-loss treatments beginning to change what and how much people buy.
I also know from experience that historical loyalty doesn’t guarantee future loyalty. The challenge for retailers isn’t simply collecting more customer data, it’s turning that data into something useful quickly enough to recognise when behaviour changes and act on it.
That becomes particularly important during the Golden Quarter, when shoppers are surrounded by Christmas offers, Black Friday messages and loyalty incentives, all competing for their attention and spend.
Timing also matters as much as targeting. Christmas spending decisions start long before December, so spotting an early change in behaviour gives retailers the chance to act before that spend goes elsewhere. We’ve run campaigns that reward shoppers for spending over a number of weeks to earn a Christmas bonus or target them with relevant offers months out to help spread the cost of the big day. It’s an approach we’re increasingly seeing retailers use to lock in festive spend early.
Blanket discounting can drive volume, but it can also mean giving away margin to people who would have bought the product anyway. Instead of asking, ‘What promotion can we send everyone?’, the better question is, ‘What would give this particular customer a reason to come back to us for their next top-up shop in a few days’ time?’
For one shopper that might be money off a regular family staple, for another, an incentive to return to a category they haven’t bought recently. At Christmas, it could mean encouraging someone to trade up to a more premium product or giving them a reason to buy more of the big-day shop with you rather than splitting that spend across several retailers. So it’s the same retailer but very different customers. That is where shopper intelligence becomes commercially useful. Here at Catalina, this is where we can really help to understand those differences so retailers can turn them into relevant action.
October marks the second year of our Long Live the Coupon campaign and National Coupon Awareness Month at Catalina, and there’s a reason the coupon remains so important to us. It’s where our story began. Back in 1983, Catalina pioneered the checkout coupon, using scanner data to give shoppers targeted offers based on what they actually bought.
More than 40 years later, the technology has changed enormously, but the principle hasn’t: understand your shopper, give them something relevant and measure whether it changed their behaviour.
Today that can happen across physical and digital channels, using real-time transaction data and advanced analytics to identify audiences, activate personalised marketing and measure what actually happened afterwards.
We analyse 15 billion transactions annually and work with more than 500 brands, but the interesting bit isn’t the size of the data, it’s what retailers can do with it.
Did that customer come back? Did they make another trip? Did they spend more? Did the activity generate incremental sales rather than simply rewarding behaviour that would have happened anyway? Those are the questions that matter commercially.
And this isn’t only a conversation for the UK’s biggest supermarkets. Smaller and regional retail chains can gain just as much from understanding their shoppers at this level. They may not have the budgets or scale of the major grocers, but they don’t need to be everything to everyone. They need to understand the customers they already have and give them compelling reasons to return.
Perhaps that’s the biggest change in loyalty. We used to think about it as something relatively fixed – win a customer, give them a card, keep them coming back. Today’s shopper has more information, more offers and more reasons to look around, and our research suggests they’re doing exactly that.
So this Golden Quarter, I’d be asking how many of your loyalty scheme members are genuinely choosing you, what will bring them back again next week, and how much more of their Christmas spend you could win.
If you want to win more shopper loyalty this Golden Quarter, it’s not too late. We can help you turn customer insight into action and give shoppers a reason to choose you again. Come and talk to us.
For more information, please visit: National Coupon Awareness Month 2026
Details can be found on Catalina UK’s official LinkedIn page

items.title: ﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? | Michael Jacobs
items.summary: This is a chance for the PM to advance his progressive agenda and tackle urgent issues such as AI regulation and climate action Among the many crucial decisions Andy Burnham has to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year. Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities. Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime minister Continue reading...
items.body:
Among the many crucial decisions Andy Burnham has to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year.
Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities.
The last time the UK chaired the forum was in 2009, when Gordon Brown presided over the rescue of the global economy after the financial crash. Before the London summit in April 2009, the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, had wrung his hands, saying that “none of us has a plan”. Barack Obama had a quick response to this: “Gordon has a plan.”
He did. Brown got the G20 to agree to a $5tn fiscal stimulus among its member states, increase International Monetary Fund lending to developing countries and create a new global coordinator for financial regulation, the Financial Stability Board.
But 2009 was a rare year for the G20, in that it actually achieved something. In general, the long communiques issued at its annual leaders’ summits reflect only the lowest-common-denominator agreement on broad principles. The G20 rarely commits its members to doing anything they were not planning to do anyway, and only occasionally makes genuinely collective decisions. One of the most consequential was the suspension of developing countries’ debt during the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the subsequent establishment of a “common framework” for debt treatment.
Indeed, for what is meant to be the effective executive committee of the global economy, the G20 is an oddly weak institution. Its 19 members (plus the EU and the African Union) have no HQ or staff and do not even have a standing website: if you want to know what the G20 has agreed over the past 20 years you need to go to a set of unofficial webpages hosted by some enterprising academics at the University of Toronto.
For most countries, hosting the G20 summit is a chance to impress its domestic audience by showing that its head of government bestrides the world stage. Last year Donald Trump boycotted it; the South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, was glad simply to get any kind of agreed communique. This year, the US is the host, with one of Trump’s own properties near Miami the summit venue in December: expect a show of personal and US power and very little attempt to achieve anything by way of multilateral cooperation.
But that makes Burnham’s task next year even more critical. The UK needs to show that it is still possible for the world’s leading nations – including the US and China – to work together to meet the key challenges facing the world.
So what should the UK’s presidency priorities be?
First, agreement on the need for, and a process towards, a global treaty on the regulation of artificial intelligence. After the recent alarm over the existential risks of AI, the UK has a chance to lead the world towards a global agreement on its control. Even if Trump is unwilling to sign up, getting the rest of the world to do so, seeking a form of global “technological security”, would be a vital achievement. A future US president might well wish to accede later.
Second, acknowledgment of the growing risk to food security and a plan to deal with it. The incoming “supersized” El Niño weather pattern is combining with the climate crisis, soil and biodiversity loss, and the impact of the war in the Middle East on diesel and fertiliser costs to create a perfect storm for the world’s food system. Agricultural yields are falling and food prices rising, leaving millions of people at risk of hunger. The G20 needs to act to prevent it.
Third, acknowledgment of accelerating climate insecurity – the severe risks posed by the climate emergency to all countries’ economies and societies – and agreement on coordinated measures to improve climate resilience. Though the Trump administration does not support emissions reduction, it does accept the need to adapt to climate change, and this year’s extreme weather events have impressed on all governments how urgent this is. The G20 should agree to provide more support to the most vulnerable countries.
Fourth, agreement on a debt restructuring programme for low- and middle-income economies whose debt – through no fault of their own, but because of rising global interest rates – has now become unsustainable. For too many countries the compounding of debt burdens with rising energy and food prices has made sustainable economic growth all but impossible.
What connects these issues is that all are global problems that can only be tackled through international cooperation. They each address aspects of national and global security – technological, food, climate and economic. Importantly, the first three address problems that are highly visible and politically salient to the British public, enabling the government to demonstrate how international action benefits people at home. (And the fourth represents a vital contribution to global economic growth.) And all have a good chance of being agreed in the G20, despite the conflicts and tensions that in other areas divide the world’s leaders.
G20 host countries always invent a slogan to express their presidency ambitions. In other contexts Burnham has said he wants to give people a sense of hope. That is something people all over the world need. For the G20 he might wish to try “national security through international cooperation”. It would not be a bad legacy to aim for.
- Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime minister

items.title: We generate £1M for the economy from every 10,000 fans: O2 and Wembley Arena call for business rates cut
items.summary: Representatives for venues including Wembley Arena, the O2 and Alexandra Palace have made the case to the Treasury to extend a reduction on business rates to bigger sites.
items.body:
We generate £1M for the economy from every 10,000 fans: O2 and Wembley Arena call for business rates cut
Major music arenas have urged Andy Burnham to offer them some respite on business rates, in line with smaller venues, ahead of the Budget.
Representatives for venues which include Wembley Arena, the O2 and Alexandra Palace have made the case to the Treasury to apply a 20 per cent reduction in business rates to all live music venues next year.
The Prime Minister has already announced support for pubs and grassroots music venues from next April, as well as promising ‘further’ action to fix the unfair tax system.
In a submission to the Treasury ahead of the Budget, industry group LIVE said that an extension of relief would ‘mean more activity on our high streets.’
It cited research from the National Arenas Association which claims that every 10,000 visitors at a concert will spend at least £1million in the local economy.
Popstars including RAYE, Ariana Grande and Lily Allen have performed at the O2 Arena this year so far while country music megastar Kacey Musgraves is among those set to take to the stage at Wembley Arena, the stadium’s smaller sister venue, over the next few months.
Major music venues - including the O2, which has seen singers such as Raye perform this year - have asked the Government to be included in a scheme for cheaper business rates.
LIVE chief executive Jon Collins said there was a ‘strong economic case’ for the expansion as total consumer spend related to concerts hit a record £7.6 billion last year.
He added: ‘Arenas fill hotels, bars and restaurants and generate significant spending on our high streets, while smaller arenas - many of which are council-owned - face similar pressures as grassroots venues. It makes little sense to recognise that contribution while excluding some of the venues generating it.’
Business rates are set to be a pivotal area for Chancellor John Healey and Burnham to prove they are listening to firms at the Budget on October 28.
It comes after former chancellor Rachel Reeves faced a fierce backlash over her botched business rates reforms announced last year that saw Labour MPs banned from pubs and many industries facing punishing hikes in their bills.
The live music industry also wants a shake-up in the way venues’ rateable values – part of the formula for calculating a property’s final bill – are determined.
Burnham has already announced an independent review into how pubs’ rates are calculated, led by business rates expert Jerry Schurder. He will report back in March 2027.
But music venues also want to be included in such a review. LIVE told the Treasury that values are calculated ‘using assumptions designed for fundamentally different businesses.’
It added: ‘The current system does not reflect how venues actually operate. We have fixed capacities, limited trading hours and high staffing costs, and rely on touring artists outside our control.’
‘This creates a disconnect between our tax liabilities and commercial reality, constraining venues' potential to further support Government’s economic growth ambitions.’
A Treasury spokesman said: ‘As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.’
