Jysk rolls out Enactor powered unified commerce platform in Norway with Holland and Belgium next
Danish home furnishing retailer Jysk has gone live in Norway with its Enactor powered unified commerce platform. It has spent the last couple of months transitioning all 110 of its stores in the country to the new platform.
This integrates all store systems into one unified solution, with the aim of making everyday processes simpler and more efficient for both colleagues and customers.
“We now have several points of sale throughout the store, which means we can help customers and process payments wherever they are. My team has done an amazing job, and they really love the new way of working. It has been great to see how quickly it has become a natural part of our daily routines,” says Connie Evensen, Store Manager at Jysk Furuset in Oslo.
Sweden and Finland joined the new platform a couple of weeks ago, and the Netherlands and Belgium are up next.
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Unified commerce will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

items.title: Deliveroo teams with Coco on launch of food and grocery on demand delivery robots in some parts of the UK
items.summary: Deliveroo is gearing up to roll-out delivery robots, supplied by US company Coco, in the UK. These will be used for takeaways and groceries, with Deliveroo claiming that the robots will not replace human riders but rather complement them during off peak hours. Canary Wharf, Milton Keynes, Leeds, Stockton-on-Tees, and Nottingham are the initial areas to get the service, with plans afoot for a broader UK roll-out. Deliveroo runs a three-sided marketplace across roughly restaurants, grocers and retailers, all promising delivery in as little as 30 minutes. It is also a DoorDash subsidiary now, after being taken over by the US giant in a deal valuing the business at £2.9 billion. So this move shouldn’t come as a huge surprise. The announcement follows its rival Just Eat partnering earlier this year with Starship Technologies to roll-out a pilot scheme involving self-driving delivery robots in North East Barnsley. Deliveroo is gearing up to roll-out delivery robots, supplied by US company Coco, in the UK. These will be used for takeaways and groceries, with Deliveroo claiming that the robots will not replace human riders but rather complement them during off peak hours.
Canary Wharf, Milton Keynes, Leeds, Stockton-on-Tees, and Nottingham are the initial areas to get the service, with plans afoot for a broader UK roll-out.
Deliveroo runs a three-sided marketplace across roughly restaurants, grocers and retailers, all promising delivery in as little as 30 minutes. It is also a DoorDash subsidiary now, after being taken over by the US giant in a deal valuing the business at £2.9 billion. So this move shouldn’t come as a huge surprise.
The announcement follows its rival Just Eat partnering earlier this year with Starship Technologies to roll-out a pilot scheme involving self-driving delivery robots in North East Barnsley.
Mert Öztekin, Chief Technology Officer at Just Eat, said at the time of the launch: “Our ground robotics trials are all about innovating to improve the customer experience. We’ve teamed up with a diverse range of local independent restaurants to trial the Starship robots and we’ll be listening to their feedback closely, as well as that of our customers.”
Ahti Heinla, Founder and Chief Executive of Starship Technologies, added: "Our little robots have been providing a much loved service to communities across the UK since 2018, and we're excited to launch in Barnsley with Just Eat today.”
“Barnsley is exactly the kind of community we built Starship for - where technology serves people ethically and respectfully. We’re confident locals will enjoy the quick convenience our robots bring, making life a little easier for people. They’re polite and friendly, and they can’t wait to make new friends!”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
On demand delivery will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

items.body:
Evri tests out two-legged delivery robot in Barnsley: last week’s biggest retail technology plays
RTIH rounds up the stand out retail technology deals, launches, deployments and pilots from the past seven days. Including OpenAI, Walmart, JD Sports, Stüssy, Woolworths Group, Lincolnshire Co-op, JB Hi-Fi, Vusion, Morrisons, StrongPoint ALS, VoCoVo, Iceland Foods, Healthy Options, THG Fulfil, and AutoStore.
Evri
Evri has launched what is pitched as Europe's first trial of a two-legged autonomous delivery robot, bringing the technology to Barnsley, the UK's first government backed Tech Town.
The trial, in partnership with Japan-based Refined Robotics, will explore how robotics can support couriers, enhance customer choice and help shape the future of parcel delivery.
The two-legged robot has been designed specifically for outdoor last mile deliveries. It can carry parcels weighing up to 15kg, travel at speeds of up to 6km/h and navigate real-world environments that can be challenging for traditional autonomous technologies, including climbing stairs, traversing uneven surfaces and entering and exiting delivery vans.
The robot can operate autonomously or be remotely monitored and is capable of both attended and unattended deliveries to help ensure consumers never miss a parcel. Throughout the trial, Evri will evaluate how the technology performs in residential environments and how it could support operational efficiency while maintaining the high levels of service customers expect.
OpenAI and Walmart
A dress spotted on social media, an outfit for an autumn wedding or a new style to try: OpenAI is adding tools to ChatGPT that let shoppers move from an idea to an image of themselves wearing it, with Walmart among the retailers involved from launch.
The new Virtual Try On and Favorites features allow users to visualise clothing and accessories using their own photographs, then save products to return to later. Shoppers can describe what they want, upload an image of an item or use a screenshot as the starting point for a search.
Walmart is bringing its fashion range into the experience. Daniel Danker, EVP AI Acceleration, Product, and Design, said on LinkedIn that the US retail giant was working with OpenAI “from day one” to make its fashion available through Virtual Try On, Shop this Look and Favourites.
Sharing an example himself, he added: “Found something I like. Think I should I buy it?”
Morrisons
Morrisons has launched a pilot of StrongPoint ALS’s temperature controlled Click & Collect lockers at the retailer’s Skipton store in North Yorkshire.
The aim here is to provide a convenient and flexible way to collect ambient, chilled and frozen groceries.
In a LinkedIn post, Christopher Evison, Senior Productivity Manager at Morrisons, said: “This is a great step forward for Click & Collect at Morrisons. It brings faster pickups - orders are pre-packed in paper bags and loaded into the lockers in advance. Simply enter your unique six-digit code when you arrive and go. And more flexibility - the lockers are helping us extend operating hours by two hours a day, giving customers even more options for when they collect. Freshness is guaranteed - the multi-temperature lockers can accommodate ambient, chilled and frozen products, whether customers are picking up a few essentials or their full weekly shop.”
He added: “There is also support when you need it - integrated VoCoVo headsets provide a direct two-way connection to store colleagues, making it easy to get assistance or complete any required ID checks. Huge thank you to all that have supported from both StrongPoint and Vocovo. It’s another great step forward in investing in our online proposition while keeping customer convenience at the heart of what we do. A huge well done to everyone involved in getting the launch over the line - a fantastic team effort. We’re really looking forward to seeing customers using the lockers and continuing to drive our online propostion forward.”
Lidl GB
Lidl is rolling out new self-checkouts across its UK stores which play video footage back to customers while they are scanning their shopping. These will be deployed in all new stores and retrofitted into existing locations.
They will feature built in overhead cameras, vertically mounted large format screens, and LED lights to alert staff if people need help while scanning their shopping. To leave, customers must scan a receipt printed by the machine at a gate at the exit.
Roll-out is also taking place across hundreds of Lidl and Kaufland stores in Germany.
A Lidl spokesperson told RTIH: “The new self-checkouts are designed to be more customer friendly, enhancing the shopping experience while boosting efficiency.”
Diamantis Masoutis
Diamantis Masoutis is expanding its implementation of electronic shelf labels (ESL) in partnership with Mobile Technology, Vusion's partner in Greece. The initiative leverages Vusion's platform. In the first phase, Masoutis installed the company’s cloud-based ESL platform in 28 stores.
Theodoros Gerostergioudis, CEO at Diamantis Masoutis, says: "Digital transformation is a strategic priority for Masoutis. Our goal is to build strong and sustainable foundations that will reinforce our operational excellence, empower our people, and continuously enhance the value we offer our customers. Through targeted investments and reliable partnerships, we are shaping a resilient, future oriented retail model."
Apostolos Doxanidis, IT Director at Diamantis Masoutis, comments: "Electronic shelf labels represent an important step in our company's digital transformation journey. Technology does not replace the contribution of our people - it supports them with modern tools, so they can focus on service and on improving the consumer experience. With respect for our team and a vision for the future, we continue to invest in innovations that improve day-to-day operations and quality of service."
Tote
Tote AI has launched HQ Genie AI, with the aim of bringing a ChatGPT/Claude like experience to retail operations. It says that, instead of digging through dashboards and static reports, operators can ask questions of their live business data and get answers in seconds, with the system beginning to move beyond answering questions to monitoring operations and taking action.
This is in production with Loop Markets, Huck’s and Spinx.
Users can type questions such as what the latest discount on Diet Soda is, how many Monster Energy drinks a given store has left, what daily sales looked like over the last ten days, or the status of a specific card refund. As Tote runs the Point of Sale, HQ Genie draws on operational data from across the store, including the devices connected through Tote Device Cloud, which lets corporate help desk teams use it to spot and diagnose problems. For example, a help desk analyst can ask which devices across the chain need attention and see where issues are occurring, store by store.
Agentic workflows, now in beta, are built into HQ Genie and work to automate recurring tasks.
Halfords
Halfords has unveiled Pulse, the retailer’s new internal communications platform, powered by Blink. Designed to connect colleagues across the entire Halfords Group, Pulse brings together communications, recognition, resources, and key tools into one mobile first experience.
A spokesperson for Halfords said: “Whether colleagues are serving customers in our stores and garages, supporting operations in our distribution centres, or working behind the scenes from our support centres, the Blink platform provides a simpler way for our One Halfords Family to stay informed, connected, and engaged.”
“A huge thank you to the Blink team for their partnership throughout the project. Their expertise, innovative solutions, and collaborative approach have helped turn a shared vision into reality, and their support has been invaluable from planning through to launch. We're also incredibly grateful to the many Halfords colleagues who have contributed to bringing Pulse to life - this has been a true cross-functional, team effort driven by a shared ambition to create a better colleague experience for everyone.”
They added: “Today is just the beginning, and we're excited to see colleagues across the group start connecting, sharing, recognising, and celebrating together on Pulse. Helping our One Halfords Family stay connected and keep the nation moving, together.”
Paula Rosa Manhattan
Dassault Systèmes reports that Paula Rosa Manhattan, a kitchen specialist in the UK and part of Ballingslöv International, will use its HomeByMe solution to launch a new offering that delivers kitchens directly to customers for the first time.
“Adopting Dassault Systèmes’ HomeByMe Smart Kitchen Planner is a transformative step for our business as we embrace e-commerce to meet the evolving expectations of today’s consumers,” says Richard Lee, CEO at Paula Rosa Manhattan. “As manufacturers, we’ve always been focused on quality and craftsmanship. Now, we’re taking our expertise directly to customers by offering them a fully digital experience that they control. HomeByMe will support this natural step for us, with a simple, guided design experience for our customers.”
“Paula Rosa Manhattan’s decision to integrate HomeByMe Smart Kitchen Planner as a backbone of their new business strategy demonstrates its whish to explore new ways to engage with consumers,” says Annabel Chaussat, CEO, 3DVIA, Dassault Systèmes. “Digital transformation of the buying journey is becoming essential to enhance consumer experiences and drive growth in the kitchen sector. Paula Rosa Manhattan is adapting to changing markets in the UK kitchen sector, bringing a new kitchen design and selling experience.”
Stüssy
Stüssy is partnering with RELEX Solutions to connect forecasting, replenishment and merchandise financial planning across its global operations. RELEX will support the streetwear brand across stores, e-commerce and distribution centres (DCs).
Stüssy designs and markets men’s and women’s apparel and accessories, with products sold through its own stores as well as skate, surf, department and specialty retailers. The company operates a business spanning North America, Europe and Asia. As it grows its global operations, connecting demand, inventory and financial planning across channels have become increasingly important.
RELEX will support forecasting and replenishment alongside open to buy and merchandise financial planning. This will give teams better visibility into demand and lost sales, helping sharpen future buying decisions and improve sales and seasonal sell-through through stronger demand forecasting. Stüssy has selected Neos by Argon, a RELEX partner, to help bring the planning approach into operation across its network.
“Stüssy knows where it wants to take its planning organisation and has set a clear bar for what success looks like,” says Frank Lord, Chief Revenue Officer at RELEX Solutions. “Better visibility into customer demand will help the team make more informed buying decisions and plan with confidence and we’re excited to support them as they build for the next stage of growth.”
THG Fulfil and AutoStore
THG Fulfil, a fulfilment operating system from THG Ingenuity, has announced the expansion of its distribution partnership with AutoStore. The expanded tie up extends its distribution authorisation beyond a robotics as a service (RaaS) model to include traditional CapEx ownership, with the aim of giving brands and retailers greater commercial flexibility when investing in warehouse automation.
THG Fulfil operates 796 AutoStore robots across its own fulfilment network and has integrated the AutoStore system with its own proprietary WCS, to deliver over 11,000 bins to picking stations per hour and cut average pick wait times by 78%. That experience underpinned its recent AutoStore build for Footasylum, comprising 85 AutoStore R5 robots across more than 96,000 bin locations, storing the retailer’s entire live SKU range.
The expanded agreement gives THG Fulfil global distribution rights for the entire AutoStore product range under the CapEx model, while its RaaS offering covers a selected range of AutoStore products, including R5 Pro and R5 Pro+ robots, CarouselPort, ConveyorPort and VersaPort.
Lincolnshire Co-op
The Barcode Warehouse is working with Lincolnshire Co-op on the roll-out of a new self-checkout solution. Lincolnshire Co-op, which operates more than 220 outlets across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties, including food stores, pharmacies, post offices and travel branches, is expanding self-service checkout options across its food store estate as part of its investment in enhancing customer experience.
Andy Warman, Chief Commercial and Transformation Officer at Lincolnshire Co-op, says: “The introduction of self-checkouts across our food stores represents an important step in enhancing the shopping experience for our customers. Working with The Barcode Warehouse, we have delivered a solution that provides greater convenience, reduces queuing times, and gives customers more choice in how they shop. This investment reflects our ongoing commitment to continuing to deliver high standards of customer service and embracing innovation technology that adds value for our communities.”
The Barcode Warehouse has supplied and supported the retailer's in-store technology estate for more than three years. Today, it supplies Point of Sale equipment, handheld devices for stock management and pricing updates, reduced to clear printing solutions and managed services support across the business.
Hozelock
Polytag has partnered with Hozelock, a manufacturer of garden watering and outdoor products, to introduce smart QR codes across its garden product range. The deployment brings connected product experiences to the garden and outdoor sector for the first time.
By scanning the codes, Hozelock customers can access product specific guidance, including how to guides and videos, while the company gains new insight into how and where its products are being used.
The smart QR codes, powered by Polytag's platform, have been added to Hozelock products available through retailers including B&Q. When scanned, the codes can direct consumers to content tailored to their market and device language, enabling Hozelock to provide relevant information across its international markets using a single QR code.
This is particularly valuable for Hozelock's range of technical and higher value garden products, where packaging alone cannot always display the level of information customers may need. The digital connection also provides a foundation for future product level information requirements, including Digital Product Passports, allowing Hozelock to build on the infrastructure already in place as these requirements are rolled out.
The deployment also gives Hozelock visibility beyond the point of purchase. Through the Polytag platform, the company can see where and when customers are engaging with its products, providing data that was previously unavailable once a product had left the retailer.
Dike & Son
Independent retailer Dike & Son Superstore says it has achieved a 92% sell-through rate on reduced products, according to its latest weekly September figures. That is up from around 73% when it joined Gander in February 2026.
The increase of around 19 percentage points follows improvements to the way the store manages reductions, alongside promotion of Gander through its Facebook page. In the latest reporting week, Dike & Son sold 1,200 of the 1,310 products it reduced.
Adam Vincent, Company Director at Dike & Son, says: “Our team has worked hard to make reductions a consistent part of how we operate and we have also used Facebook to let customers know they can find great value through Gander. Seeing our sell-through rise from around 73% in February to 92% in our latest weekly figures is a fantastic result. It shows what our colleagues can achieve when the right technology is backed by good processes in-store.”
H&M
H&M has overhauled its onsite search across more than 60 markets, working with Voyado. The retailer says that the move away from keyword matching to an intent driven model has reduced soft exits (where shoppers drift off because of friction rather than choice) by 80% and cut customer exits from search by 30%.
Rather than matching search terms to product names, the new setup reads a range of signals at once: stock availability, add to bag actions, purchase behaviour, product newness, revenue performance and customer intent and updates rankings in real-time.
“As our business grew, we needed a more intelligent approach to search, ranking, and discovery. We found Voyado to be the best fit for us.” says Lars Gezelius, Acting Global Head of Digital at H&M.
Erica Sandelin Ekelund, CEO at Voyado, says: "Search is a clear signal of what customers actually want. When a customer searches, they’re not browsing - they’re telling you. And many retailers are throwing that signal away. H&M recognised the value and used it to rebuild their customer experience from the ground up, and the numbers confirm they were right. The most successful retailers won’t be those with the most extensive catalogues. They’ll be the ones who understand their customers and what they actually came for.”
Woolworths Group
Pine Labs has extended its technology partnership with Woolworths Group. Through its Qwikcilver subsidiary, Pine Labs powers the technology platform supporting Woolworths' gift card programmes. The tie up will build on this foundation, with a focus on strengthening platform capabilities, enabling deeper technology integration, and supporting the evolution of gift card experiences across physical and digital channels.
“The most valuable technology partnerships are built over time and become part of the infrastructure that businesses rely on every day,” says B Amrish Rau, CEO at Pine Labs. “Over the past five years, Pine Labs and Woolworths have established that kind of relationship. We are now expanding the technology foundation with enhanced platform capabilities that can support new gift card experiences and stored-value use cases.”
He adds: “As gift card experiences become increasingly digital, integrated, and omnichannel, enterprises need technology infrastructure that can evolve alongside customer expectations. Our partnership with Woolworths is focused on providing that long-term foundation.”
JB Hi-Fi
Vusion has announced a new roll-out initiative at Australian retailer JB Hi-Fi’s stores. Under the agreement, JB Hi-Fi plans to deploy Vusion’s digital shelf-edge technology in Australia following a pilot phase, as well as a full roll-out across its New Zealand store network.
“We are focused on innovation that delivers efficiencies to our store operations and supports our teams in serving customers,” says Cameron Trainor, MD at JB Hi-Fi Australia. “Our collaboration with Vusion gives us a scalable technology platform to support store teams, strengthen execution and advance the next phase of our strategy.”
“We are very proud to support JB Hi-Fi as it takes this important step toward a more connected store network,” says Pierre Demoures, SEVP & COO at Vusion. “Australia is a key market for Vusion and JB Hi-Fi is one of the region’s most distinctive retailers. This agreement shows how connected store infrastructure can help leading retailers modernise operations while preserving the store experience that makes them unique.”
JD Sports
Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, has taken to social media to provide an update on the retailer’s RFID programme, which involves various countries and thousands of stores.
In a LinkedIn post, McGrath said: “This week, our final country goes live with RFID, Germany. And with that, everything we directly control will be live for phase one of our RFID programme. When I look back at what we’ve achieved, the numbers are pretty incredible: 1,000 stores directly launched in 14 months. And across the wider global group, working alongside our counterparts around the world: 2,700 stores live out of 4,800 in that same period, 192 stores a month!”
He added: “But the numbers only tell part of this story. RFID isn’t just about scanners, tags and technology. It’s about changing behaviours, processes and mindsets. We’ve done things that were uncomfortable. Challenged established ways of working. Asked people to rethink processes they’d used for years. And, most importantly, brought people with us on the journey. And we haven't done that alone.”
Musgrave Northern Ireland
Musgrave Northern Ireland, part of the Musgrave Group, an Irish convenience retail, wholesale and food service business, whose brands include SuperValu and Centra, has expanded its rapid grocery delivery offering through a partnership with Snappy Technologies, powered by the company’s Order Aggregation (OA) platform.
This connects its stores with leading rapid delivery marketplaces, with five company owned SuperValu and Centra stores across Northern Ireland now available on Just Eat and Uber Eats. A further 13 company owned stores are expected to launch in the next phase of the roll-out across September.
With the OA platform, Musgrave can manage orders from multiple online marketplaces through a single, streamlined solution. The technology enables retailers to manage key functions including orders, menus, promotions and stock across multiple channels.
Iceland Foods
Iceland Foods has partnered with Retail Insight to deploy its AI powered WasteInsight solution as part of the retailer's focus on reducing food waste.
General Manager of EMEA and APAC at Retail Insight, Martin Rigby, says: "Retailers have access to more operational data than ever before, but data only creates value when it enables better decisions. The opportunity is to move from reporting what has already happened to identifying where action is needed before waste occurs.”
"We are delighted to be working with Iceland to support its continued focus on reducing food waste. By combining AI with operational insight, WasteInsight helps surface the products and actions that matter most, enabling colleagues to intervene earlier and with greater confidence."
Iceland Foods’ Stores Director, Steve Shirley, says: "Reducing food waste remains an important priority for Iceland. We are continually looking at ways to improve how we use operational data to support our colleagues in making faster, better informed decisions in stores.”
"Working with Retail Insight will help us explore how AI driven operational intelligence can support our waste reduction objectives while improving consistency across our store operations."
Kesko
Finnish retailing conglomerate, Kesko, is building a new logistics centre in Nurmijärvi, Finland, and has selected KNAPP as its automation partner for the first phase of the project. Kesko is a grocery retailer and wholesaler and its new central warehouse in Nurmijärvi is being built for the company’s foodservice business for the hotel, restaurant and catering (HoReCa) sector. Construction work began at the beginning of 2026.
“We are building an automation solution designed to serve our business for decades to come,” says Pekka Tala, Development Director at Kesko. “That is why it was important for us to find a solution that not only meets today’s needs, but also enables us to develop our operations in the future.”
According to Tala, the fundamentals of logistics automation have remained similar in many respects, but system performance and reliability have advanced considerably. Software also plays a growing role, as automation solutions guide operations more intelligently than before.
Kesko and KNAPP have worked together previously, and a joint planning process reinforced the view that KNAPP’s solution is well aligned with the objectives set for the logistics centre. The single facility must be able to serve different customers and order types efficiently using the same technology platform.
Healthy Options
Healthy Options, a Philippines’ retailer of natural and organic products, has expanded its use of RELEX Solutions’ platform, adding price optimisation, fresh optimisation, and pick to zero capabilities across its stores and distribution centres. The implementation is being delivered in partnership with Genie X.
The retailer first deployed RELEX forecasting and replenishment capabilities in October 2025, consolidating supply chain planning across thousands of SKUs. Healthy Options had been managing pricing through manual, spreadsheet-based processes that made it difficult to react quickly to market shifts.
As the company has grown, so has the complexity of balancing competitive pricing with margin protection and its positioning as a premium quality retailer. Price Optimisation will give Healthy Options access to price elasticity data to support pricing calls that keep the business customer centric without eroding margins.
Fresh Optimisation will support the retailer in reducing waste, improving availability, and ensuring its fresh assortment consistently meets the quality standard customers expect. By running forecasting, replenishment, pricing, and fresh optimisation on a unified AI driven platform, it says it will be able to make more connected decisions across its operations.

items.body:
Dragons' Den star Touker Suleyman's new beauty brand Lipstick London gets physical at Westfield
Lipstick London, a new beauty brand from Touker Suleyman, Owner and Chairman at Hawes & Curtis and Ghost, has launched a kiosk at Westfield London, White City.
In a LinkedIn post including a photo of himself at the shopping centre, the fashion retail entrepreneur and TV personality, best known for his stint on reality show Dragons’ Den, said: "Here we are this morning (Saturday, 3rd) launching my new brand Lipstick London at Westfield I want to thank everyone queuing up for this new movement. 15 months of hard work has gone into this. Let’s go."
RTS 2026
“Technology is an overhead. It’s expensive if you don’t use it properly,” Suleyman said at Retail Technology Show 2026 in London earlier this year.
In conversation with Kate Hardcastle, Suleyman used his slot at RTS 2026 on 22nd April to encourage the thousands of retailers attending “not to give up” during the present tough times and recommended harnessing technology in the right way, namely, to enable: Manpower reductions and better cost control; Improve decision-making power; Enhance customer insights and service, citing CRM systems as “important in this area”.
In regard to AI, which was inevitably a hot topic at RTS 2026, Suleyman said: “My question is does it help the bottom line? Does it help with staffing costs, marketing, targeting and so on?”
“AI is running too fast,” he added. “If I was an SME I’d sit on the fence and see how it develops. You’ve got to find the bit of AI that actually helps you.” Otherwise, it’s just another overhead without sufficient return on investment. He reminded those in the audience that cashflow should still be king, especially for small to medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that are facing rising rents, taxes, employment costs and regulation, while their consumers simultaneously suffer a renewed cost of living crisis.
“However, the fundamentals of retail in sales, expense control, and a focus on profit and loss don’t change,” added Suleyman, while stressing nor does the way to success. This is achieved by making sure you focus tightly on: Ongoing excellent service; Value; Awareness of the competition.
“If you can survive in retail, you can survive anywhere. But you must work hard,” said Suleyman, while also bemoaning the planned UK governmental addition of digital passports and ID work validity checks as “a new cost overhead”.
“The price will come down though in my opinion,” he added, “so don’t sign up yet to expensive fancy solutions.”
Also at RTS 2026, Suleyman described Lipstick London as "Charlotte Tilbury at half the price...I’ve duped luxury brands after spending a year researching the marketplace thoroughly, empowering a chemist, and so on. It’s made in China … and will be available in two flagship stores in London’s West End; eight to ten kiosks in shopping centres like Westfield; and online.”
Lipstick London will deploy guerilla marketing tactics for its autumn launch, providing 10,000 online and social media ambassadors with free product that they will help evangelise for. “There are 300,000 pieces of product being offered as well, which is a cheaper way to get customers than giving it to Meta, Google or any of those others.” The cost of acquisition is a live issue in retail at the moment and this is one possible response.
The passion to succeed still burns bright in Suleyman, it seems. But the direct to consumer Beauty Pie rival dupe brand already exists. It may be a tough potential competitor, albeit in the D2C arena without stores, and often with bland packaging.
Regardless, Suleyman has had enough success to think he can make a go of Lipstick and his shirt collar and high end outfitter, Hawes & Curtis. As he himself advised: “Don’t give up!”

Constructor claims a first as it launches Agentic Checkout solution powered by Stripe
Constructor, which powers search and product discovery for retailers including Sephora, The Very Group, Monica Vinader, White Stuff, and Furniture Village, has launched Agentic Checkout, a move that, the company claims, makes it the first to offer Stripe powered checkout directly within an onsite shopping agent.
People on retail sites and apps can discover products, ask questions, get personalised recommendations, and refine their choices, then check out and pay, without leaving the agent experience. They can pay via the Link By Stripe digital wallet or other payment methods.
Agentic Checkout is available within Constructor’s AI Shopping Agent (ASA), which lets shoppers describe what they need in natural language and get guidance based on their context, history and intent, and AI Product Insights Agent (PIA), which answers product specific questions directly on product detail pages. Agentic Checkout will expand to more touchpoints throughout retailers’ digital properties later this year.
“The promise of agentic commerce is that a shopper can express what they need and AI can help them every step of the way, making every part of the journey easier, more helpful, and more enjoyable,” says Eli Finkelshteyn, CEO and Co-founder at Constructor.
“Delivering on that promise requires best-in-class discovery and then best-in-class checkout. Constructor has spent years focused on improving the discovery experience and helping shoppers find the right products, while Stripe has built world class payments infrastructure that helps shoppers buy those products easily and securely. Together, we’re making agentic shopping more complete for consumers and more valuable for retailers.”

items.body:
Walmart addresses shopper pricing and AI concerns: last week's most read retail technology articles
Check out our most clicked retail technology articles from last week, including H&M, Voyado, Fanatics, The Barcode Warehouse, Lincolnshire Co-op, Lidl GB, Morrisons, StrongPoint ALS, VoCoVo, JD Sports, OpenAI, Destro AI, and the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
H&M overhauls onsite search across more than 60 markets in technology partnership with Voyado
H&M has overhauled its onsite search across more than 60 markets, working with Voyado. The retailer says that the move away from keyword matching to an intent driven model has reduced soft exits (where shoppers drift off because of friction rather than choice) by 80% and cut customer exits from search by 30%.
Rather than matching search terms to product names, the new setup reads a range of signals at once: stock availability, add to bag actions, purchase behaviour, product newness, revenue performance and customer intent and updates rankings in real-time.
“As our business grew, we needed a more intelligent approach to search, ranking, and discovery. We found Voyado to be the best fit for us.” says Lars Gezelius, Acting Global Head of Digital at H&M.
Erica Sandelin Ekelund, CEO at Voyado, says: "Search is a clear signal of what customers actually want. When a customer searches, they’re not browsing - they’re telling you. And many retailers are throwing that signal away. H&M recognised the value and used it to rebuild their customer experience from the ground up, and the numbers confirm they were right. The most successful retailers won’t be those with the most extensive catalogues. They’ll be the ones who understand their customers and what they actually came for.”
Fabeltics exec and CX and AI specialist Jack Roberts joins RTIH Innovation Awards judging panel for 2026
We're hugely pleased to announce the addition of Jack Roberts to the judging panel for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards. Jack is Senior Global Director of GMS Technology at Fabletics, where he leads the global technology strategy supporting customer experience across its portfolio of brands.
With more than 15 years of industry experience, Jack has led large scale transformation across customer engagement, automation and AI, with a focus on translating emerging technology into measurable business and customer outcomes. His work has received international industry recognition, and he is a regular conference speaker and customer advisory board member, contributing to the wider conversation on the future of customer experience and AI.
Welcome onboard, Jack!
Further information on our judging panel can be found here. In addition to Jack, it includes representatives from Ingka Group/Ikea, JD Sports Fashion, Batteries Plus, Holland & Barrett, Walmart, CVS Health, Amazon, Boots, C&C Group, Warner Bros. Discovery, East of England Co-op, PoundFun, Austen & Blake, and Gordon Ramsay Restaurants.
The NFL lands on London's Oxford Street as Fanatics opens pop-up store for 2026 London games
The National Football League and Fanatics, the league's official retail partner, have opened an NFL Shop pop-up retail store on London's Oxford Street, as American football returns to the capital for three games this October.
Located at 360-366 Oxford Street, the 1,000 sq ft store will be open from Thursday, 1st October, to Monday, 19th October, spanning all three 2026 NFL London games: the Indianapolis Colts vs. Washington Commanders on 4th October and the Philadelphia Eagles vs. Jacksonville Jaguars on 11th October, both at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, followed by the Houston Texans vs. Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium on 18th October.
Fans can shop official NFL jerseys and an assortment of merchandise across NFL teams, alongside a range of products available exclusively in London. The Oxford Street store will also host NFL Shop LIVE!, a programme of fan events. On opening night, Thursday, 1st October, NFL UK legend Efe Obada will sit down with broadcaster Neil Reynolds to talk about his NFL career and new charity project. On Thursday, 8th October, Phoebe Schecter and Neil Reynolds will record an NFL London Games special of "Inside the Huddle" in front of a live audience. Both events start at 6 p.m., with limited seating available on a first come, first served basis.
The store at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium will also become an official NFL Shop from Saturday, 3rd October to Sunday, 11th October, across both Tottenham games, with a number of exclusive collections available in-store. It opens with an NFL Shop Tottenham Family Day on Saturday, 3rd October, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., with games, prizes, exclusive merchandise and special guests.
JD Sports updates on RFID programme as Germany goes live and 1,000 stores milestone is reached
Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, has taken to social media to provide an update on the retailer’s RFID programme, which involves various countries and thousands of stores.
In a LinkedIn post, McGrath said: “This week, our final country goes live with RFID, Germany. And with that, everything we directly control will be live for phase one of our RFID programme. When I look back at what we’ve achieved, the numbers are pretty incredible: 1,000 stores directly launched in 14 months. And across the wider global group, working alongside our counterparts around the world: 2,700 stores live out of 4,800 in that same period, 192 stores a month!”
He added: “But the numbers only tell part of this story. RFID isn’t just about scanners, tags and technology. It’s about changing behaviours, processes and mindsets. We’ve done things that were uncomfortable. Challenged established ways of working. Asked people to rethink processes they’d used for years. And, most importantly, brought people with us on the journey. And we haven't done that alone.”
The Barcode Warehouse teams with Lincolnshire Co-op on self-checkouts roll-out across food stores
The Barcode Warehouse is working with Lincolnshire Co-op on the roll-out of a new self-checkout solution. Lincolnshire Co-op, which operates more than 220 outlets across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties, including food stores, pharmacies, post offices and travel branches, is expanding self-service checkout options across its food store estate as part of its investment in enhancing customer experience.
Andy Warman, Chief Commercial and Transformation Officer at Lincolnshire Co-op, says: “The introduction of self-checkouts across our food stores represents an important step in enhancing the shopping experience for our customers. Working with The Barcode Warehouse, we have delivered a solution that provides greater convenience, reduces queuing times, and gives customers more choice in how they shop. This investment reflects our ongoing commitment to continuing to deliver high standards of customer service and embracing innovation technology that adds value for our communities.”
The Barcode Warehouse has supplied and supported the retailer's in-store technology estate for more than three years. Today, it supplies Point of Sale equipment, handheld devices for stock management and pricing updates, reduced to clear printing solutions and managed services support across the business.
Lidl deploys new self-checkouts that show UK shoppers on screens across retailer's store network
Lidl is rolling out new self-checkouts across its UK stores which play video footage back to customers while they are scanning their shopping. These will be deployed in all new stores and retrofitted into existing locations.
They will feature built in overhead cameras, vertically mounted large format screens, and LED lights to alert staff if people need help while scanning their shopping. To leave, customers must scan a receipt printed by the machine at a gate at the exit. Roll-out is also taking place across hundreds of Lidl and Kaufland stores in Germany.
A Lidl spokesperson told RTIH: “The new self-checkouts are designed to be more customer friendly, enhancing the shopping experience while boosting efficiency.”
Morrisons partners with StrongPoint ALS and VoCoVo on Click & Collect pilot at Skipton store
Morrisons has launched a pilot of StrongPoint ALS’s temperature controlled Click & Collect lockers at the retailer’s Skipton store in North Yorkshire.
The aim here is to provide a convenient and flexible way to collect ambient, chilled and frozen groceries.
In a LinkedIn post, Christopher Evison, Senior Productivity Manager at Morrisons, said: “This is a great step forward for Click & Collect at Morrisons. It brings faster pickups - orders are pre-packed in paper bags and loaded into the lockers in advance. Simply enter your unique six-digit code when you arrive and go. And more flexibility - the lockers are helping us extend operating hours by two hours a day, giving customers even more options for when they collect. Freshness is guaranteed - the multi-temperature lockers can accommodate ambient, chilled and frozen products, whether customers are picking up a few essentials or their full weekly shop.”
He added: “There is also support when you need it - integrated VoCoVo headsets provide a direct two-way connection to store colleagues, making it easy to get assistance or complete any required ID checks. Huge thank you to all that have supported from both StrongPoint and Vocovo. It’s another great step forward in investing in our online proposition while keeping customer convenience at the heart of what we do. A huge well done to everyone involved in getting the launch over the line - a fantastic team effort. We’re really looking forward to seeing customers using the lockers and continuing to drive our online propostion forward.”
Walmart joins OpenAI's ChatGPT fashion push as Virtual Try On and Favourites launch
A dress spotted on social media, an outfit for an autumn wedding or a new style to try: OpenAI is adding tools to ChatGPT that let shoppers move from an idea to an image of themselves wearing it, with Walmart among the retailers involved from launch.
The new Virtual Try On and Favourites features allow users to visualise clothing and accessories using their own photographs, then save products to return to later. Shoppers can describe what they want, upload an image of an item or use a screenshot as the starting point for a search.
Walmart is bringing its fashion range into the experience. Daniel Danker, EVP AI Acceleration, Product, and Design, said on LinkedIn that the US retail giant was working with OpenAI “from day one” to make its fashion available through Virtual Try On, Shop this Look and Favourites.
Sharing an example himself, he added: “Found something I like. Think I should I buy it?”
'Next wave of AI will be physical': Warehouse robotics startup Destro AI bags $8 million in seed funding
Destro AI, which is building a shared intelligence layer for warehouse robotics, has raised $8 million in seed funding co-led by Base10 Partners and Bonfire Ventures, with participation from CoFound Partners. The funding will accelerate deployment of Destro’s platform across enterprise warehouses and expand the company’s engineering and research teams.
“Everyone is building capable robots,” says Manthan Pawar, Founder and CEO at Destro AI. “We believe the next breakthrough won’t come from another robot. It will come from the intelligence layer that enables any robot to work together. Customers aren’t buying robots; they’re investing in throughput, reliability, and business outcomes. That’s what we’re building.”
Destro has built two complementary AI systems: MothershipOS and Vision OS. MothershipOS is pitched as the shared mind outside the robot body, intelligently deciding which robot should perform which task, where, when, and how, to optimise complex warehouse workflows. VisionOS is an on-robot intelligence platform that enables complex mobile manipulation using AI models trained from human demonstrations, allowing robots to better perceive, grasp, and interact with real-world environments.
Walmart head honcho John Furner looks to draw a line in the sand on AI, technology and pricing
John Furner, President and CEO at Walmart, has written an open letter to the US retail giant's customers about AI and pricing. "For more than 50 years, our pricing principle has been Every Day Low Prices (EDLP). Prices can change. We lower them when we can pass savings along. Sometimes they rise because an item costs more to buy or transport,” he writes.
“But using someone’s income, shopping history or moment of need to charge them more would violate the EDLP promise our business model is built on. We won’t do it. YOU are at the heart of our why and our relationship with you has always been built on trust. For decades, our associates have built that trust, one interaction at a time. So, as technology improves, we’re putting the same attention on trust and serving you as we do when you walk into our stores and clubs."
He adds: "I've heard concerns about companies using that information and technology to charge you more. want to tell you where we stand: We price the product, not the person. Many of you have seen the digital shelf labels in our stores and some have asked why we have them. A shelf price should match what rings up at checkout. Digital shelf labels help us do that more consistently by displaying the right price. They also save associates time replacing paper tags. It may sound like an easy task, but as someone who has had to change those paper tags by hand over the years, I can tell you it’s a time-consuming and unrewarding task. Our associates would much rather be helping you, our customers."
AI, Furner notes, has added new ways for Walmart to serve its customers and members. But there are also questions about the information it has access to.
“Understanding our customers and members is what makes us special and allows us to better serve them. For years, that has taken place in our stores and clubs as we help each customer with their individual needs. We want to offer that same level of personalised care when our customers shop online with Sparky, our AI shopping assistant. When you engage with Sparky, that’s an invitation to serve you better, not to use your personal information to set a personalised price. We’ve never used the relationships our associates have with customers to charge more, and we won’t do that with AI,” Furner says.
He concludes: “With that in mind, I want to share three commitments you can count on as technology changes: We don't set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won't. Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won't change the price. And whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it's never a reason to charge you more. We'll hold our shopping tools to the same promise.”
“We won't use the information you share with us on Sparky or otherwise to raise your price or hide lower priced options that meet your needs. We’ll continue to use your information responsibly and respect your choices. You decide whether to share additional details for more personalised help. We’ll continue to be clear about how we use that information, protect it and honor the choices you make. When you do share, we will focus that data on ways that better serve you. Our people will continue to oversee pricing, and we'll monitor and test our technology against these commitments.

Shaftesbury Capital reports that beauty and wellness brand Kiehl’s has opened a new European flagship space, at 43 Carnaby Street in London. items.body:
Specsavers research: UK high street still plays a vital role in people’s lives and to their healthcare
Just 10% of Brits put hearing in their top three health priorities, and only 7% say that they invest most of their time and money in it compared to other areas of their health, according to new research from Specsavers.
A survey of 2,000 UK consumers, reveals that 35% consider eye health to be important, but only 28% invest their time and money in it - pointing to a gap between importance and investment that persists across every generation.
Brits rank sleep, diet, exercise and mental health above their sight and hearing, despite the fact that losing either sense can have lifelong consequences. And the scale of the problem is growing - new analysis from Development Economics commissioned by Specsavers has found that sight loss cases will rise from 2.38 million to 3.11 million by 2040. As well as this, 19.2 million adults have hearing loss in the UK today, and cases of significant hearing loss are expected to rise by 16% by 2040.
Part of the issue is that Brits are hesitant to get tested - 50% wouldn’t book a test unless something felt wrong, and 47% of those assume that their sight and hearing are fine until symptoms show. This is despite many recognising the importance of sight and hearing care to their overall wellbeing.
While they may not feel that they need to get tested right away, the amount of people living with sight and hearing loss by 2040 is projected to rise by millions. And according to the British Academy of Audiology, of the 6.7 million UK adults experiencing hearing loss that could benefit from a hearing aid, only around two million currently use one. Hearing and sight issues already costs the UK £106 billion - this is projected to rise to £126 billion by 2040 if changes aren’t made to the accessibility of care within communities.
The research has uncovered that time and proximity are key barriers stopping people getting their hearing and sight tested. People don’t travel more than 30 minutes for a sight or hearing test, with 28% reporting that lack of time is contributing to their delaying or avoiding an eye test, and 22% feeling the same way when it comes to a hearing test.
The high street still plays a vital role in people’s lives and to their healthcare. 90% say that opticians are essential to their high street, making it the same importance as the post office or bank, and daily high street visitors are three times more likely to get their sight and hearing tested than people who rarely go (73% of regular high street visitors get tested compared to 26% of non-regulars).
Carina Hummel, Managing Director Optics UK&ROI at Specsavers, says: “Regardless of where people live or their circumstances, it’s so important that we create and preserve easy access to quality sight and hearing care. We need to encourage people to treat their eye and ear health the same way they would treat other areas of their health - a routine check-up, not just booking an appointment when something feels “off”.
“Offering easy access to care via high street appointments and home visits improves health outcomes and wellbeing, ensuring that we are looking after ourselves. For adults, that looks like having a sight test every two years, and a hearing test every 18 months to two years for people over 40. Appointments don’t take long and can ultimately help to detect and treat any conditions sooner.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
High street retailers will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.

items.body:
Could AI agents become the next digital employees in retail?
Retailers have spent years adding new digital tools for payments, e-commerce, customer service and inventory management. AI agents could introduce a different kind of technology: software that does not only provide information, but can also follow workflows and complete defined tasks.
Platforms such as Agensi.io add another layer to this development by offering SKILL.md skills that give compatible AI agents specialised instructions. That raises an interesting question for retailers: could these agents eventually function more like digital employees than conventional software?
In short
AI agents can support retail teams with repeatable digital work such as organising product information, preparing customer responses, researching competitors and reviewing content. Skills make these agents more specialised because they define how a particular task should be approached. The most realistic model is therefore not an autonomous AI employee that runs a department, but several agents that each perform a clearly defined role under human supervision.
AI agents are moving beyond the chatbot
Generative AI first entered many workplaces through chat interfaces. A retailer could ask for a product description, analyse some information or draft a customer email. The AI produced an answer, but the employee remained responsible for providing instructions and moving the work through every subsequent stage.
An agent can take on a broader workflow. It can receive a goal, break that goal into steps and use available tools or information to work towards a result. This distinction matters in retail because many digital activities consist of recurring processes rather than isolated questions.
What turns a general AI agent into a retail specialist?
A general AI model might understand what merchandising or customer service means, but that does not automatically make it suitable for a retailer's specific workflow. It does not inherently know which checks should happen before a product goes live, how a customer complaint should be escalated or which information should be included in a particular analysis.
SKILL.md provides a way to encode such instructions. A skill is essentially a structured instruction file that teaches a compatible agent how to perform a particular task. Unlike a temporary prompt, the skill can remain available for repeated use. This allows the underlying AI to stay general while its working method becomes much more specific.
Skills can become job descriptions for AI agents
The comparison with employees becomes useful here. A new employee might bring general knowledge to a role, but still needs procedures, responsibilities and standards before performing company-specific work. Skills can play a similar role for agents.
A code review skill, for example, can specify what an agent should check and how findings should be reported. The same principle can extend beyond development. Skills can encode workflows for research, documentation, content planning or other repeatable knowledge tasks. Multiple skills can also be combined, giving one agent different procedures depending on the work it receives.
Three retail roles an AI agent could support
Retail offers plenty of opportunities to apply this model because digital commerce produces large amounts of repetitive information work. Three examples show how the same general AI could perform very different roles once its instructions change.
A merchandising agent
A merchandising agent could collect product performance information, organise findings and flag products that deserve attention. A dedicated skill could determine which information needs to be considered and how the results should be structured. The merchandiser can then concentrate on decisions about positioning, promotions and assortment rather than assembling the initial analysis.
A customer service agent
A service agent could classify incoming questions, retrieve relevant information and prepare responses for common situations. Its skill could define the required checks and indicate when a case must be escalated. Employees would still handle sensitive complaints and unusual circumstances, while the agent deals with more predictable preparation work.
A product data agent
Large catalogues create repetitive tasks around categories, descriptions and missing product attributes. A product data agent could inspect this information according to predefined rules and flag inconsistencies before publication. Human approval can remain part of the process while the agent handles much of the initial checking.
Which retail tasks suit AI agents?
The strongest candidates usually have a repeatable process and a result that employees can verify. The distinction becomes clearer when tasks are separated from the decisions surrounding them.
This division prevents the discussion from becoming a simple choice between humans and AI. A retailer can automate part of a workflow without handing over the entire responsibility.
Repeatable skills could matter more than clever prompts
Prompts work well for individual tasks, but they become less practical when employees repeatedly need to explain the same process. A skill can preserve those instructions and make them available when a relevant request appears.
This also creates consistency between users. A team could share the same skill instead of every employee developing a different collection of prompts. Agensi's material describes project-level skills as a way to encode shared standards and workflows so that agents can apply them across a team. That principle could become increasingly relevant as businesses move from individual AI experimentation towards repeatable agent workflows.
More autonomy requires tighter permissions
A product description agent and a pricing agent should not necessarily have the same access. The first may only need product information, while the second could potentially interact with commercially sensitive data or systems where a mistake has immediate consequences.
Retailers therefore need to define permissions alongside skills. A skill explains how a job should be performed, but access determines what the agent is actually able to do. Human approval can remain mandatory for actions involving payments, customer data, pricing or other decisions with larger consequences.
Could AI agents replace retail employees?
AI agents are more likely to automate parts of retail jobs than complete roles. Retail work involves judgement, negotiation, physical activity, customer relationships and responses to circumstances that do not fit neatly into predefined procedures. Agents are better suited to work where the process can be described and the output can be checked.
The term "digital employee" therefore works best as a functional comparison. An agent can have a role, instructions and boundaries, but responsibility still sits with the people operating the business.
Retail teams could become mixed teams
The next stage may involve several specialised agents rather than one AI assistant attempting every task. A retailer could have one agent supporting merchandising, another checking product data and another preparing customer service work. Each could use different skills and permissions while operating around the same business systems.
That structure resembles a small digital team. The difference is that retailers can introduce it workflow by workflow. They do not need to automate an entire department before discovering whether the approach works.
Skills could become a new layer in retail technology
Retail technology has traditionally focused on systems that store information, process transactions or help employees analyse what is happening. AI agents introduce the possibility that software can also perform parts of the work that follow from that information.
Skills could make that development more practical by giving agents repeatable procedures instead of relying on fresh instructions every time. The retailer still has to decide which processes deserve automation, what information an agent can access and where employees must intervene. If those boundaries are clear, the digital employee may arrive quietly: not as a replacement behind the counter, but as a specialised agent taking care of clearly defined work.

items.title: British government ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’
items.summary: Experts say country does not have plan to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for future shortages Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham. The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is “complacent about food as a national security matter”. Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004. Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports. Realign national food production around nutritional needs. Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes. Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply. Continue reading...
items.body:
Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham.
The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is “complacent about food as a national security matter”.
Academics, business leaders, community groups and food partnerships are urging the new government to treat food as a national security issue and work to make the UK’s food system more resilient, in a era when food supplies “can be weaponised”, they caution.
The signatories warn that the “just-in-time” delivery system built up over recent decades “is not fit for today’s or tomorrow’s challenges”, as little stock is held along the food supply chain and the UK does not have any national food storage. Ministers wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s.
“The food system is exposed to shocks and threats from geopolitics, climate heating, ransomware, energy outages, software malfunction and disinformation,” according to the letter.
The experts go on to warn: “These shocks will fall upon a system that is highly wasteful, import-dependent, environmentally unsustainable, and driven by the pursuit of private profit rather than resilience, with millions of people unable to afford a decent, healthy diet.”
The letter calls on ministers to do the following.
- Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004.
- Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports.
- Realign national food production around nutritional needs.
- Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes.
- Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply.
The warning comes weeks after the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog, issued a rebuke to ministers, accusing them of failing to do enough to help households and businesses plan for possible emergencies.
The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, while the UK is more reliant on food imports than some of its neighbours.
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, recently recommended that UK households build up stores of enough food and water to survive a few days without power or water, amid warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a wet, stormy winter to the UK.
The letter claims the government is not paying enough attention to what such a store should look like, and is failing to consider that many lower-income households may not be able to afford to build up a stockpile.
One of the signatories, Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, said: “We need a system shift: grow more food; more regionalism, diversity and storage at multiple levels, not just households; and public engagement in civil food defence. Central government must provide more strategic leadership while encouraging actions at different levels. Communities and households cannot resolve faultlines in the UK’s food system.”
Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who also signed the letter, said: “Food resilience, healthy diet and environmental benefits all point in the same direction: grow more of the vegetables, fruit and pulses people actually need, closer to home.”
The Cabinet Office is to launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for future emergencies.
The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include assembling items at home that could include tinned meat, fruit or vegetables that do not need cooking.
Eagle has said she would oversee farming improvements and a reservoir-building programme that should help Britain face extreme weather.
